articles.title: Boolean structure of a valuation
articles.statement:
Given a valuation $v$ assigning a Boolean to each
atom, the Boolean structure of $v$ is the structure for the first-order language of
propositional atoms whose domain is the set of Booleans $\{\mathrm{false}, \mathrm{true}\}$
and in which the nullary relation symbol of an atom $a$ holds exactly when $v(a)$ is true.
The language has no function symbols, so nothing else needs to be interpreted.

articles.title: Embedding propositions as first-order sentences
articles.statement:
The translation of propositions over a
type of atoms into sentences of the first-order language of propositional atoms, defined by
recursion: an atom $a$ becomes the atomic sentence given by the nullary relation symbol of $a$,
and $A \wedge B$, $A \vee B$ and $A \to B$ become the conjunction, the disjunction and the
implication of the translations of $A$ and $B$.

articles.title: First-order language of propositional atoms
articles.statement:
For a type of atoms, the first-order
language whose relation symbols are exactly one nullary relation symbol for each atom, with
no relation symbols of positive arity and no function symbols.

articles.title: Relation symbols of the propositional language
articles.statement:
For a type of atoms, the family of
relation symbols indexed by arity that consists of one nullary relation symbol for each atom
$a$ and has no relation symbols of positive arity.

articles.title: The embedding of propositions preserves truth-table semantics
articles.statement:
For every valuation $v$
assigning a Boolean to each atom and every proposition $A$, the first-order sentence obtained
by embedding $A$ is true in the Boolean structure of $v$ if and only if the truth-table value
of $A$ under $v$ is true.

articles.title: Cut
articles.statement:
Let $\Gamma$ be a finite list of formulas of a first-order language $L$ with free
variables in $\alpha$, let $\varphi$ and $\psi$ be such formulas, and write $\varphi, \Gamma$ for
the list $\Gamma$ with $\varphi$ added in front. If $\Gamma \vdash \varphi$ and
$\varphi, \Gamma \vdash \psi$ in natural deduction, then $\Gamma \vdash \psi$.

articles.title: Natural deduction
articles.statement:
Fix a first-order language $L$ and a type $\alpha$ of variables;
formulas and terms below are those of $L$ with free variables in $\alpha$. For a formula
$\varphi$ with one additional bound variable and a term $t$, write $\varphi[t]$ for $\varphi$
with $t$ substituted for that bound variable and $\forall \varphi$ for its universal
quantification. Write $\neg \psi$ for $\psi \to \bot$, and $\psi, \Gamma$ for the list $\Gamma$
with $\psi$ added in front. Derivability $\Gamma \vdash \varphi$ of a formula $\varphi$ (the
conclusion) from a finite list $\Gamma$ of formulas (the open hypotheses) is the least relation
closed under the following rules.

* Assumption: $\Gamma \vdash \varphi$ whenever $\varphi$ is a member of $\Gamma$.
* Implication introduction: from $\varphi, \Gamma \vdash \psi$ infer
  $\Gamma \vdash \varphi \to \psi$.
* Implication elimination: from $\Gamma \vdash \varphi \to \psi$ and $\Gamma \vdash \varphi$
  infer $\Gamma \vdash \psi$.
* Reductio ad absurdum: from $\neg \varphi, \Gamma \vdash \bot$ infer $\Gamma \vdash \varphi$.
* Universal introduction: if a variable $x$ occurs free in no member of $\Gamma$ and does not
  occur free in $\varphi$, then from $\Gamma \vdash \varphi[x]$ infer
  $\Gamma \vdash \forall \varphi$.
* Universal elimination: from $\Gamma \vdash \forall \varphi$ infer $\Gamma \vdash \varphi[t]$,
  for every term $t$.
* Reflexivity: $\Gamma \vdash t = t$ for every term $t$.
* Substitution: from $\Gamma \vdash s = t$ and $\Gamma \vdash \varphi[s]$ infer
  $\Gamma \vdash \varphi[t]$.

articles.title: Existential introduction
articles.statement:
Let $\Gamma$ be a finite list of formulas of a first-order
language $L$ with free variables in $\alpha$, let $\varphi$ be such a formula with one
additional bound variable, let $t$ be a term, and write $\varphi[t]$ for $\varphi$ with $t$
substituted for that bound variable. If $\Gamma \vdash \varphi[t]$ in natural deduction, then
$\Gamma \vdash \exists \varphi$, where $\exists \varphi$ abbreviates $\neg \forall \neg \varphi$
as in Mathlib.

articles.title: Soundness for theories
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a theory, that is, a set of sentences of a
first-order language $L$, and regard each sentence of $T$ as a formula with free variables in
$\alpha$. If a formula $\varphi$ with free variables in $\alpha$ is provable from these
formulas, then $\varphi$ holds in every model of $T$ under every assignment of elements of the
model to the variables in $\alpha$.

articles.title: Weakening
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be an infinite type of variables, let $\Gamma$ and $\Delta$ be
finite lists of formulas of a first-order language $L$ with free variables in $\alpha$ such that
every member of $\Gamma$ is a member of $\Delta$, and let $\varphi$ be such a formula. If
$\Gamma \vdash \varphi$ in natural deduction, then $\Delta \vdash \varphi$.

articles.title: Consistency of the calculus
articles.statement: The empty context does not derive `⊥`.

articles.title: Provability from a set of formulas
articles.statement:
A set $T$ of formulas of a first-order language $L$
with free variables in $\alpha$ proves such a formula $\varphi$ when there is a finite list
$\Gamma$ of members of $T$ with $\Gamma \vdash \varphi$ in natural deduction.

articles.title: Injective relabeling preserves derivability
articles.statement:
Let $f \colon \alpha \to \beta$ be an
injective map between types of variables. For a formula $\psi$ of a first-order language $L$
with free variables in $\alpha$, write $f(\psi)$ for Mathlib's relabeling of $\psi$ by $f$,
which replaces each free variable $x$ by $f(x)$, and for a finite list $\Gamma$ of such formulas
write $f(\Gamma)$ for the list obtained by applying this to each member of $\Gamma$. If $\Gamma$
is such a list, $\varphi$ is such a formula and $\Gamma \vdash \varphi$ in natural deduction,
then $f(\Gamma) \vdash f(\varphi)$.

articles.title: Injective renaming preserves derivability
articles.statement:
Let $f \colon \alpha \to \beta$ be an
injective map between types of variables. For a formula $\psi$ of a first-order language $L$
with free variables in $\alpha$, write $f(\psi)$ for the renaming of the free variables of
$\psi$ by $f$, and for a finite list $\Gamma$ of such formulas write $f(\Gamma)$ for the list
obtained by renaming each member of $\Gamma$. If $\Gamma$ is such a list, $\varphi$ is such a
formula and $\Gamma \vdash \varphi$ in natural deduction, then $f(\Gamma) \vdash f(\varphi)$.

On formulas this renaming coincides with Mathlib's relabeling of free variables.

articles.title: Soundness of first-order natural deduction
articles.statement:
Let $\Gamma$ be a finite list of formulas of
a first-order language $L$ with free variables in $\alpha$, and let $\varphi$ be such a formula.
If $\Gamma \vdash \varphi$ in natural deduction, then for every $L$-structure $M$ and every
assignment $v \colon \alpha \to M$ under which all members of $\Gamma$ hold, $\varphi$ holds
under $v$.

articles.title: Symmetry of equality in natural deduction
articles.statement:
Let $\Gamma$ be a list of first-order formulas
and let $s$ and $t$ be terms. If the equation $s = t$ is derivable from the hypotheses $\Gamma$,
then the equation $t = s$ is derivable from $\Gamma$.

articles.title: Transitivity of equality in natural deduction
articles.statement:
Let $\Gamma$ be a list of first-order
formulas and let $r$, $s$ and $t$ be terms. If the equations $r = s$ and $s = t$ are both
derivable from the hypotheses $\Gamma$, then the equation $r = t$ is derivable from $\Gamma$.

articles.title: Relabelling a formula is renaming
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a first-order language and
$f : \alpha \to \beta$ a map. For every $L$-formula $\varphi$ with free variables in $\alpha$ (a
bounded formula with no bound variables), Mathlib's relabelling of $\varphi$ along $f$ equals the
renaming of the free variables of $\varphi$ along $f$.

articles.title: Symbols of a formula
articles.statement:
The set of function and relation symbols of a first-order
language $L$ that occur in a formula $\varphi$ (with free variables and possibly bound
variables), defined by recursion on $\varphi$: falsum $\bot$ contributes no symbols, an
equation $t_1 = t_2$ contributes the symbols of the terms $t_1$ and $t_2$, an atomic formula
$R(t_1, \dots, t_k)$ contributes $R$ together with the symbols of the terms $t_i$, an
implication $\varphi \to \psi$ contributes the symbols of $\varphi$ and of $\psi$, and
$\forall x\, \varphi$ contributes the symbols of $\varphi$. Variables and the equality sign
contribute nothing.

articles.title: Free variables of a renamed formula
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a first-order language and
$f : \alpha \to \beta$ a map. For every bounded $L$-formula $\varphi$ with free variables in
$\alpha$ and $n$ bound variables, the set of free variables of the renaming of $\varphi$ along $f$
is the image under $f$ of the set of free variables of $\varphi$.

articles.title: Instantiation commutes with the universal quantifier
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a first-order language,
$t$ an $L$-term with free variables in $\alpha$, and $\varphi$ a bounded $L$-formula with free
variables in $\alpha$ and $m + 2$ bound variables. Instantiating $t$ in the universal formula
$\forall \varphi$ (which has $m + 1$ bound variables) gives the universal quantification of the
instantiation of $t$ in $\varphi$.

Under a quantifier the outermost bound variable is still index $0$ (bound variables are de Bruijn
levels), so instantiation passes through the quantifier unchanged.

articles.title: Instantiation shifts the remaining bound variables down
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a first-order language,
$t$ an $L$-term with free variables in $\alpha$, and $i < m$. Instantiating $t$ in the term
consisting of the bound variable $i + 1$ (a term with free variables in $\alpha$ and $m + 1$ bound
variables) gives the term consisting of the bound variable $i$ (with $m$ bound variables).

articles.title: Instantiation at the outermost bound variable
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a first-order language, $t$ an
$L$-term with free variables in $\alpha$, and $m$ a natural number. Instantiating $t$ in the term
consisting of the bound variable $0$ (a term with free variables in $\alpha$ and $m + 1$ bound
variables) gives $t$, regarded as a term with free variables in $\alpha$ and $m$ bound variables.

articles.title: Instantiating the outermost bound variable of a term
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a first-order language,
$t$ an $L$-term with free variables in $\alpha$, and $s$ an $L$-term with free variables in
$\alpha$ and $m + 1$ bound variables $0, \dots, m$. The instantiation of $t$ in $s$ is the term
with free variables in $\alpha$ and $m$ bound variables obtained from $s$ by substituting $t$ for
the bound variable $0$, replacing each other bound variable $i + 1$ by $i$, and leaving the free
variables unchanged.

articles.title: Instantiating the outermost bound variable of a formula
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a first-order
language, $t$ an $L$-term with free variables in $\alpha$, and $\varphi$ a bounded $L$-formula with
free variables in $\alpha$ and $m + 1$ bound variables $0, \dots, m$. The instantiation of $t$ in
$\varphi$ is the bounded formula with free variables in $\alpha$ and $m$ bound variables obtained
from $\varphi$ by instantiating $t$ in every term of its atomic subformulas: in each term, $t$ is
substituted for the bound variable $0$ and each other bound variable $i + 1$ is replaced by $i$.
Falsum, implication and universal quantification are kept, the quantifier being passed through
unchanged since bound variables are de Bruijn levels.

articles.title: Relabeling variables preserves the leaf count
articles.statement: Relabeling variables does not change the number of leaves.

articles.title: Leaf count of a first-order term
articles.statement:
The number of leaves of a first-order term.

Variables and nullary function applications are leaves. A nonnullary function application has
the sum of the leaf counts of its arguments.

articles.title: Truth of a universal formula
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a first-order language, $M$ an $L$-structure,
$v : \alpha \to M$ an assignment of the free variables, and $\varphi$ a bounded $L$-formula with
free variables in $\alpha$ and one bound variable. Then the formula $\forall \varphi$ holds in $M$
under $v$ if and only if, for every $a \in M$, $\varphi$ holds in $M$ under $v$ with its bound
variable set to $a$.

articles.title: Truth depends only on the free variables
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a first-order language, $M$ an
$L$-structure, and $\varphi$ a bounded $L$-formula with free variables in $\alpha$ and $n$ bound
variables. If two assignments $v, v' : \alpha \to M$ agree on every free variable of $\varphi$,
then for every choice of values in $M$ for the $n$ bound variables, $\varphi$ holds in $M$ under
$v$ and these values if and only if it holds under $v'$ and these values.

articles.title: Truth of an instance
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a first-order language, $M$ an $L$-structure,
$v : \alpha \to M$ an assignment of the free variables, $t$ an $L$-term with free variables in
$\alpha$, and $\varphi$ a bounded $L$-formula with free variables in $\alpha$ and one bound
variable. Then the instantiation of $t$ in $\varphi$, a formula with free variables in $\alpha$,
holds in $M$ under $v$ if and only if $\varphi$ holds in $M$ under $v$ with its bound variable set
to the value of $t$ under $v$.

articles.title: Truth of a renamed formula
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a structure for a first-order language $L$, let
$f : \alpha \to \beta$, and let $\varphi$ be a bounded formula of $L$ with free variables in
$\alpha$ and $n$ bound variables. For every assignment $v : \beta \to M$ of the free variables
and every assignment $x : \mathrm{Fin}\,n \to M$ of the bound variables, the renaming of
$\varphi$ along $f$ holds in $M$ at $v$ and $x$ if and only if $\varphi$ holds in $M$ at
$v \circ f$ and $x$.

articles.title: Relabeling along $f$ agrees with renaming
articles.statement:
Let $f : \alpha \to \beta$ and let $\varphi$
be a bounded formula of a first-order language with free variables in $\alpha$ and $k$ bound
variables. Mathlib's relabeling of $\varphi$ along the map $\alpha \to \beta \sqcup \mathrm{Fin}\,0$
sending $a$ to the free variable $f(a)$ replaces each free variable $a$ by $f(a)$ and produces a
formula with $0 + k$ bound variables. This formula equals the renaming of $\varphi$ along $f$,
regarded as a formula with $0 + k$ bound variables through the inclusion $k \le 0 + k$.

articles.title: Renaming that fixes the free variables
articles.statement:
If a map $f : \alpha \to \alpha$ fixes every free
variable of a bounded formula $\varphi$, then renaming the free variables of $\varphi$ along $f$
leaves $\varphi$ unchanged.

articles.title: Renaming free variables of a term
articles.statement:
Given a map $f : \alpha \to \beta$ and
$n \in \mathbb{N}$, a term of a first-order language over the variables
$\alpha \sqcup \mathrm{Fin}\,n$ (free variables from $\alpha$, bound variables from
$\mathrm{Fin}\,n$) becomes a term over $\beta \sqcup \mathrm{Fin}\,n$ by replacing each free
variable $a$ with $f(a)$ and leaving the bound variables unchanged.

articles.title: Renaming free variables of a formula
articles.statement:
Given a map $f : \alpha \to \beta$, a bounded formula
$\varphi$ of a first-order language $L$ with free variables in $\alpha$ and $n$ bound variables
becomes a bounded formula of $L$ with free variables in $\beta$ and the same $n$ bound variables,
by replacing each free variable $a$ with $f(a)$ in every term of $\varphi$ and leaving the bound
variables, the relation symbols and the logical connectives and quantifiers unchanged.

articles.title: Symbols of a term
articles.statement:
The set of symbols of a first-order language $L$ that occur in a
term $t$ (with free variables and possibly bound variables), defined by recursion on $t$: a
variable contributes no symbols, and $f(t_1, \dots, t_k)$ contributes the function symbol $f$
together with the symbols of the terms $t_i$. The result lies in the set of all symbols of $L$,
but only function symbols can occur in a term.

articles.title: Eliminating a solved variable lowers the number of variables
articles.statement:
Let $x$ be a variable,
$t$ a term in which $x$ does not occur, and $E$ a list of equations. Applying the substitution
that replaces $x$ by $t$ (and fixes every other variable) to both sides of every equation of
$E$ gives a list of equations with strictly fewer distinct variables than the list obtained
by putting the equation $x = t$ in front of $E$.

articles.title: Composition of substitutions on first-order terms
articles.statement:
For substitutions $s$ and $t$,
the composite $s \gg t$ (first $s$, then $t$) sends each variable $x$ to the term obtained
from $s(x)$ by applying $t$ to every variable of $s(x)$.

articles.title: Lists of equations with the same unifiers satisfy the same specification
articles.statement:
Let $E$ and
$E'$ be lists of equations such that a substitution unifies $E$ exactly when it unifies $E'$.
If an optional substitution $r$ satisfies the unification specification for $E'$ (a returned
substitution $s$ unifies the list and every unifier $s'$ of it satisfies $s' = s \gg s'$,
where $s \gg s'$ applies first $s$ and then $s'$, and failure means the list has no unifier),
then $r$ satisfies the unification specification for $E$.

articles.title: The elimination step preserves the unification specification
articles.statement:
Let $x$ be a variable,
$t$ a term in which $x$ does not occur, $e$ an equation and $E$ a list of equations. Suppose
that for every substitution $s$, the two sides of $e$ become equal under $s$ exactly when
$s(x)$ equals the result of applying $s$ to $t$. Let $\sigma$ be the substitution that replaces
$x$ by $t$ and fixes every other variable, and let $E'$ be the list obtained by applying
$\sigma$ to both sides of every equation of $E$. Suppose an optional substitution $r$ satisfies
the unification specification for $E'$. Define the result $r'$ by: when $r$ returns a
substitution $s$, $r'$ returns $\sigma \gg s$, the composite that applies first $\sigma$ and
then $s$; when $r$ is failure, $r'$ is failure. Then $r'$ satisfies the unification
specification for the list with head $e$ and tail $E$.

articles.title: Total size of a list of equations
articles.statement:
The total size of a list of equations is the sum,
over all its equations, of the sizes of the two sides, where the size of a term is its number
of variable, constant and node symbols.

articles.title: Variables of a list of equations
articles.statement:
The variables of a list of equations form the finite
set of all variables that occur on either side of any of its equations.

articles.title: Lists of equations
articles.statement:
A list of equations over constants $C$ is a finite list of pairs
$(t, u)$ of terms over $C$, each pair standing for the equation $t = u$.

articles.title: Variables of a substituted term
articles.statement:
Let $s$ be a substitution and $t$ a term. Every
variable of the term obtained by applying $s$ to $t$ is a variable of $s(y)$ for some variable
$y$ of $t$.

articles.title: Unification returns a most general unifier
articles.statement:
If the Martelli-Montanari unification
algorithm, run on a list of equations $E$, returns a substitution $s$, then $s$ is a most
general unifier of $E$.

articles.title: Most general unifier
articles.statement:
A substitution $s$ is a most general unifier of a list of
equations $E$ when $s$ unifies $E$ and every unifier $s'$ of $E$ factors through $s$, that is,
$s' = s \gg r$ for some substitution $r$, where $s \gg r$ applies first $s$ and then $r$.

articles.title: Failure is correct when the first equation has no unifier
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a list of
equations between terms and let $u = v$ be a further equation, where $u\sigma$ denotes the
result of applying a substitution $\sigma$ to $u$. If $u\sigma \ne v\sigma$ for every
substitution $\sigma$, then returning no substitution meets the unification specification for
the list obtained by putting $u = v$ in front of $E$: no substitution unifies that list.

articles.title: Absorbing a single-variable substitution
articles.statement:
Let $x$ be a variable, $t$ a term, and
$[x \mapsto t]$ the substitution replacing $x$ by $t$ and fixing every other variable. If a
substitution $\sigma$ satisfies $\sigma(x) = t\sigma$, where $t\sigma$ is the result of applying
$\sigma$ to $t$, then the composite substitution that applies $[x \mapsto t]$ first and
$\sigma$ second equals $\sigma$.

articles.title: Single-variable substitution on first-order terms
articles.statement:
For a variable $x$ and a term $t$, the
substitution $[x \mapsto t]$ sends $x$ to $t$ and every other variable $y$ to the term $y$.

articles.title: Occurs check: size bound
articles.statement:
Let $x$ be a variable and $t$ a term in which $x$ occurs, with
$t$ not the variable $x$ itself. Then for every substitution $\sigma$, the term $\sigma(x)$ has
strictly smaller size than $t\sigma$, the result of applying $\sigma$ to $t$.

Consequently the equation $x = t$ has no unifier when $x$ occurs in $t$ and $t \ne x$ (the occurs
check).

articles.title: Size of a term
articles.statement:
The size of a term is the number of symbols in it: a variable and a
constant have size $1$, and a node with subterms $l$ and $r$ has size equal to the size of $l$
plus the size of $r$ plus $1$.

articles.title: Applying a substitution to a term
articles.statement:
For a substitution $\sigma$ and a term $t$, the term
$t\sigma$ is obtained from $t$ by replacing every variable $x$ by $\sigma(x)$: a variable $x$
becomes $\sigma(x)$, a constant is unchanged, and a node with subterms $l$ and $r$ becomes the
node with subterms $l\sigma$ and $r\sigma$.

articles.title: Substitution depends only on the variables of the term
articles.statement:
If two substitutions $\sigma$
and $\tau$ agree on every variable occurring in a term $u$, then applying $\sigma$ to $u$ gives
the same term as applying $\tau$ to $u$.

articles.title: Applying a substitution to a list of equations
articles.statement:
For a substitution $\sigma$ and a list
$E$ of equations between terms, the result is the list obtained by replacing each equation
$u = v$ of $E$, in order, by $u\sigma = v\sigma$, where $u\sigma$ is the result of applying
$\sigma$ to $u$.

articles.title: A term is fixed by substituting it for a variable it avoids
articles.statement:
If the variable $x$ does
not occur in the term $t$, then applying to $t$ the substitution $[x \mapsto t]$, which replaces
$x$ by $t$ and fixes every other variable, leaves $t$ unchanged.

articles.title: Substitution
articles.statement:
A substitution is a map assigning a term to every variable, that is, a
function from the set $\mathbb{N}$ of variables to terms.

articles.title: Terms for unification
articles.statement:
For a type $C$ of constants, a term over $C$ is either a variable
$x$, indexed by a natural number $x \in \mathbb{N}$, or a constant $c \in C$, or a binary node
built from two terms $l$ and $r$.

articles.title: Soundness of unification
articles.statement:
For every list $E$ of equations between terms, if the
Martelli–Montanari algorithm returns a substitution $s$ on $E$, then $s$ unifies $E$: applying
$s$ to the two sides of any equation of $E$ gives the same term.

articles.title: Unifier of a list of equations
articles.statement:
A substitution $s$ unifies a list $E$ of equations
between terms when, for every equation $(t, u)$ in $E$, applying $s$ to $t$ and applying $s$ to
$u$ give the same term.

articles.title: Unification returns an idempotent substitution
articles.statement:
For every list $E$ of equations between
terms, if the Martelli–Montanari algorithm returns a substitution $s$ on $E$, then $s$ is
idempotent: the composite substitution that applies first $s$ and then $s$ equals $s$.

articles.title: Completeness of unification
articles.statement:
For every list $E$ of equations between terms, the
Martelli–Montanari algorithm fails on $E$ if and only if no substitution unifies $E$.

articles.title: Most generality of unification
articles.statement:
For every list $E$ of equations between terms, if the
Martelli–Montanari algorithm returns a substitution $s$ on $E$, then every substitution $s'$
that unifies $E$ equals the composite substitution that applies first $s$ and then $s'$.

articles.title: Specification of a unification result
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a list of equations between terms and
$r$ either a substitution or failure. The specification holds for $E$ and $r$ when, if $r$ is a
substitution $s$, then $s$ unifies $E$ and every substitution $s'$ that unifies $E$ equals the
composite substitution that applies first $s$ and then $s'$; and, if $r$ is failure, then no
substitution unifies $E$.

articles.title: Martelli–Montanari unification
articles.statement:
The algorithm takes a list of equations between terms and
returns a substitution or fails. On the empty list it returns the identity substitution.
Otherwise it looks at the first equation $t = u$ and the remaining list $E$. If $t$ and $u$ are
the same variable, or the same constant, the equation is dropped and the algorithm continues on
$E$; if they are two different constants, it fails. If $t$ is a variable $x$ and $u \ne x$, or
else $u$ is a variable $x$ and $t$ is not a variable, let $v$ be the other side: the algorithm
fails when $x$ occurs in $v$, and otherwise substitutes $v$ for $x$ on both sides of every
equation of $E$ and unifies the result; if that returns $s$, it returns the substitution that
applies first the replacement of $x$ by $v$ and then $s$, and if that fails, it fails. If $t$ and
$u$ are nodes with children $l_1, r_1$ and $l_2, r_2$, it continues on the list $l_1 = l_2$,
$r_1 = r_2$ followed by $E$. If one side is a constant and the other a node, it fails.

articles.title: The elimination step of unification introduces no variables
articles.statement:
Write $V(F)$ for the set
of variables of a list $F$ of equations. Let $x_0$ be a variable, $t$ a term in which $x_0$ does
not occur, $e = (e_1, e_2)$ an equation such that every variable of $t$ occurs in $e_1$ or $e_2$,
and $E$ a list of equations, and let $E'$ be obtained from $E$ by substituting $t$ for $x_0$ on
both sides of every equation. Let $s_0$ be a substitution such that, for every variable $x$,
every variable of $s_0(x)$ is $x$ or lies in $V(E')$, and let $\sigma$ be the substitution that
applies first the replacement of $x_0$ by $t$ and then $s_0$. Then for every variable $x$, every
variable of $\sigma(x)$ is $x$, occurs in $e_1$ or $e_2$, or lies in $V(E)$.

articles.title: Variables of a substituted variable occur in the substituted term
articles.statement:
For every
substitution $s$, term $t$ and variable $y$ occurring in $t$, every variable of the term $s(y)$
occurs in the term obtained from $t$ by applying $s$.

articles.title: Substituting for a variable that does not occur in the substituted term
articles.statement:
Let $x$ be a
variable and $t$ a term in which $x$ does not occur. For every term $u$, every variable of the
term obtained from $u$ by replacing each occurrence of $x$ with $t$ is a variable of $u$ or of
$t$, and is different from $x$.

articles.title: Unification introduces no new variables
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a list of equations between terms.
If the unification algorithm succeeds on $E$ and returns the substitution $s$, then for every
variable $x$, each variable of the term $s(x)$ is either $x$ itself or a variable occurring in
some equation of $E$.

articles.title: Variables of a term
articles.statement:
The variables of a term form a finite set of natural numbers,
defined recursively: the variable $x$ has the variable set $\{x\}$, a constant has no variables,
and the variables of a node with subterms $l$ and $r$ are those of $l$ together with those of
$r$.

articles.title: Universal formulas from Henkin witnesses
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be an infinite set of
variables and let $\Delta$ be a maximal consistent set of formulas with free variables in
$\alpha$. Let $\varphi(x)$ be a formula with one bound variable $x$ left open, let
$c \in \alpha$, and write $\varphi(c)$ for the result of substituting $c$ for $x$. If
$\Delta$ contains the Henkin axiom for $\forall x\, \varphi$ with witness $c$ and contains
$\varphi(c)$, then $\Delta$ contains $\forall x\, \varphi$.

articles.title: Unions of chains of consistent sets are consistent
articles.statement:
If $C$ is a nonempty family of
sets of formulas that is totally ordered by inclusion and every member of $C$ is consistent,
then the union $\bigcup C$ is consistent.

A refutation uses only finitely many hypotheses, and these all lie in a single member of $C$.

articles.title: Consistency passes to the finite-symbol sublanguage
articles.statement:
Let $F$ be a finite set of formulas
of a first-order language $L$ with free variables in $\mathbb{N}$, and let $L_F$ be the
sublanguage of $L$ on the symbols occurring in $F$, with inclusion $\iota : L_F \to L$. If $F$ is
consistent, then so is the preimage of $F$ in $L_F$: the set of formulas $\psi_0$ of $L_F$ with
free variables in $\mathbb{N}$ whose image $\iota(\psi_0)$ under the inclusion belongs to $F$.

A refutation of the preimage maps along the inclusion to a refutation of $F$.

## Sources

- H.-D. Ebbinghaus, J. Flum, and W. Thomas, *Mathematical Logic*, 2nd ed., Springer 1994, Chapter V.

articles.title: Consistent set of formulas
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a first-order language and $\alpha$ a type of
variables. A set $S$ of formulas of $L$ with free variables in $\alpha$ is consistent when $S$
does not prove $\bot$.

articles.title: Depth of a formula
articles.statement:
The depth $d(\varphi)$ of a first-order formula $\varphi$ is the
nesting height of its implications and universal quantifiers: $\bot$, equations and relation
atoms have depth $0$, the implication $\varphi \to \psi$ has depth
$\max(d(\varphi), d(\psi)) + 1$, and $\forall \varphi$ has depth $d(\varphi) + 1$.

articles.title: Enumeration of formulas with one bound variable
articles.statement:
For a language with countably many
symbols, the formulas $\varphi_0, \varphi_1, \dots$ are a fixed enumeration, chosen by choice, of
all first-order formulas with free variables in $\mathbb{N}$ and one bound variable: every such
formula is $\varphi_k$ for some $k \in \mathbb{N}$.

articles.title: Bounded formulas lift to the finite-symbol sublanguage
articles.statement:
Let $F$ be a finite set of
formulas of a first-order language $L$ with free variables in $\mathbb{N}$, and let $L_F$ be the
sublanguage of $L$ on the symbols occurring in $F$, with inclusion $\iota : L_F \to L$. Every
bounded formula $\varphi$ of $L$ with free variables in $\mathbb{N}$ and $n$ bound variables, each
of whose symbols occurs in some formula of $F$, is the image under $\iota$ of a bounded formula
of $L_F$ with free variables in $\mathbb{N}$ and $n$ bound variables.

## Sources

- H.-D. Ebbinghaus, J. Flum, and W. Thomas, *Mathematical Logic*, 2nd ed., Springer 1994, Chapter V.

articles.title: Henkin extension of a consistent set
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a language with countably many symbols
and let $S$ be a consistent set of first-order formulas with free variables in $\mathbb{N}$ such
that every free variable of every formula in $S$ is even. Then $S$ is contained in a maximal
consistent set $\Delta$ with the Henkin property: for every formula $\varphi$ with one bound
variable, if every instance $\varphi(t)$, for $t$ a term over $\mathbb{N}$, lies in $\Delta$, then
$\forall \varphi$ lies in $\Delta$.

articles.title: Lindenbaum's lemma for first-order logic
articles.statement:
Every consistent set $S$ of first-order
formulas is contained in a maximal consistent set.

articles.title: Finite satisfiability
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a first-order language, with no countability hypothesis
on its symbols. Every finite consistent set $F$ of formulas of $L$ with free variables in
$\mathbb{N}$ is satisfiable: there are a nonempty $L$-structure $M$, in the universe of the
function symbols of $L$, and an assignment $v : \mathbb{N} \to M$ under which every formula of $F$
holds.

The proof passes to the sublanguage on the finitely many symbols occurring in $F$, applies the
countable Henkin theorem there, and expands the resulting structure along the inclusion.

## Sources

- H.-D. Ebbinghaus, J. Flum, and W. Thomas, *Mathematical Logic*, 2nd ed., Springer 1994, Chapter V.

articles.title: Model existence for arbitrary languages
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a first-order language, with no
countability hypothesis on its symbols. Every consistent set $S$ of formulas of $L$ with free
variables in $\mathbb{N}$ is satisfiable: there are a nonempty $L$-structure $M$, in the larger of
the universes of the function symbols and the relation symbols of $L$, and an assignment
$v : \mathbb{N} \to M$ under which every formula of $S$ holds.

## Sources

- L. Henkin, *The completeness of the first-order functional calculus*, J. Symbolic Logic 14, 1949, 159-166; H.-D. Ebbinghaus, J. Flum, and W. Thomas, *Mathematical Logic*, 2nd ed., Springer 1994, Chapter V.

articles.title: Model existence for first-order logic
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a language with countably many symbols.
Every consistent set $S$ of first-order formulas with free variables in $\mathbb{N}$ is
satisfiable: there are a nonempty $L$-structure $M$, in the universe of the function symbols of
$L$, and an assignment $v : \mathbb{N} \to M$ under which every formula of $S$ holds.

The free variables are first doubled, which keeps the set consistent and leaves the odd variables
free for Henkin witnesses.

articles.title: Terms lift to the finite-symbol sublanguage
articles.statement:
Let $F$ be a finite set of formulas of a
first-order language $L$ with free variables in $\mathbb{N}$, and let $L_F$ be the sublanguage of
$L$ on the symbols occurring in $F$, with inclusion $\iota : L_F \to L$. Every term $t$ of $L$
whose variables are drawn from $\mathbb{N}$ and from $n$ bound variables, each of whose symbols
occurs in some formula of $F$, is the image under $\iota$ of a term of $L_F$ with variables drawn
from the same set.

## Sources

- H.-D. Ebbinghaus, J. Flum, and W. Thomas, *Mathematical Logic*, 2nd ed., Springer 1994, Chapter V.

articles.title: Symbols of the antecedent occur in an implication
articles.statement:
For bounded formulas $\varphi$ and
$\psi$ of a first-order language $L$ with free variables in $\alpha$ and $n$ bound variables,
every symbol occurring in $\varphi$ occurs in $\varphi \to \psi$.

## Sources

- D. van Dalen, *Logic and Structure*, 5th ed., Springer 2013, §3.1.

articles.title: Symbols of the consequent occur in an implication
articles.statement:
For bounded formulas $\varphi$ and
$\psi$ of a first-order language $L$ with free variables in $\alpha$ and $n$ bound variables,
every symbol occurring in $\psi$ occurs in $\varphi \to \psi$.

## Sources

- D. van Dalen, *Logic and Structure*, 5th ed., Springer 2013, §3.1.

articles.title: Finite set of symbols of a formula
articles.statement:
The finite set of function and relation symbols
occurring in a bounded formula of a first-order language $L$, defined by recursion on the
formula: $\bot$ has no symbols; an equation $t_1 = t_2$ has the function symbols of $t_1$ and
$t_2$; an atomic formula $R(t_1, \dots, t_l)$ has $R$ together with the function symbols of
$t_1, \dots, t_l$; an implication $\varphi \to \psi$ has the symbols of $\varphi$ and of $\psi$;
and $\forall \varphi$ has the symbols of $\varphi$.

## Sources

- D. van Dalen, *Logic and Structure*, 5th ed., Springer 2013, §3.1.

articles.title: Free variables of an instance
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a term and $\varphi$ a first-order formula with
$m + 1$ bound variables, and let $\varphi(t)$ be the instance obtained by substituting $t$ for the
outermost bound variable. Every free variable of $\varphi(t)$ is a free variable of $\varphi$ or a
variable of $t$.

articles.title: Language homomorphisms preserve free variables
articles.statement:
Let $h : L \to L'$ be a homomorphism of
first-order languages, and let $\varphi$ be a bounded formula of $L$ with free variables in
$\alpha$ and $n$ bound variables. The formula of $L'$ obtained from $\varphi$ by replacing each
symbol by its image under $h$ has the same free variables as $\varphi$.

## Sources

- D. van Dalen, *Logic and Structure*, 5th ed., Springer 2013, §3.1.

articles.title: Congruence for function symbols in a maximal consistent set
articles.statement:
Let $\Delta$ be a maximal
consistent set of first-order formulas with free variables in $\mathbb{N}$, let $f$ be an $n$-ary
function symbol, let $x = (x_0, \dots, x_{n-1})$ be terms over $\mathbb{N}$ and let $i < n$. For a
term $u$, write $x[i := u]$ for $x$ with its $i$-th entry replaced by $u$. If the equation
$a = b$ lies in $\Delta$, then the equation $f(x[i := a]) = f(x[i := b])$ lies in $\Delta$.

articles.title: The $k$-th Henkin axiom
articles.statement:
For a language with countably many symbols and $k \in \mathbb{N}$,
the $k$-th Henkin axiom is the Henkin axiom $\neg \forall \varphi_k \to \neg \varphi_k(c_k)$, where
$\varphi_k$ is the $k$-th formula in the enumeration of formulas with one bound variable and
$c_k$ is the $k$-th Henkin witness.

articles.title: Henkin axiom
articles.statement:
Let $\varphi(x)$ be a formula with one bound variable $x$ left open and
let $c$ be a variable; write $\varphi(c)$ for the result of substituting $c$ for $x$. The
Henkin axiom for $\forall x\, \varphi$ with witness $c$ is the formula
$\neg \forall x\, \varphi \to \neg \varphi(c)$.

articles.title: Henkin extension
articles.statement:
For a language with countably many symbols, the Henkin extension of a set
$S$ of first-order formulas with free variables in $\mathbb{N}$ is $S$ together with all Henkin
axioms, the $k$-th Henkin axiom for every $k \in \mathbb{N}$.

articles.title: Stages of the Henkin extension
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a set of first-order formulas with free variables
in $\mathbb{N}$, in a language with countably many symbols, and let $H_k$ be the $k$-th Henkin
axiom. The stages $S_k$ are defined by $S_0 = S$ and $S_{k+1} = S_k \cup \{H_k\}$, so $S_k$ is
$S$ together with $H_0, \dots, H_{k-1}$.

articles.title: Deduction theorem
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be an infinite set of variables, let $S$ be a set of
formulas with free variables in $\alpha$, and let $\varphi$, $\psi$ be such formulas. If
$S \cup \{\varphi\}$ proves $\psi$, then $S$ proves $\varphi \to \psi$.

articles.title: Adding a Henkin axiom preserves consistency
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be an infinite set of
variables and let $S$ be a consistent set of formulas with free variables in $\alpha$. Let
$\varphi(x)$ be a formula with one bound variable $x$ left open, and let $c \in \alpha$ be a
variable that occurs free neither in $\varphi$ nor in any formula of $S$. Then $S$ together
with the Henkin axiom for $\forall x\, \varphi$ with witness $c$ is consistent.

articles.title: Universal instantiation in maximal consistent sets
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be an infinite set of
variables and let $\Delta$ be a maximal consistent set of formulas with free variables in
$\alpha$. Let $\varphi(x)$ be a formula with one bound variable $x$ left open, and for a term
$t$ write $\varphi(t)$ for the result of substituting $t$ for $x$. If $\Delta$ contains
$\forall x\, \varphi$, then $\Delta$ contains $\varphi(t)$ for every term $t$.

articles.title: Substitution of equals in maximal consistent sets
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be an infinite set of
variables and let $\Delta$ be a maximal consistent set of formulas with free variables in
$\alpha$. Let $\varphi(x)$ be a formula with one bound variable $x$ left open, and for a term
$u$ write $\varphi(u)$ for the result of substituting $u$ for $x$. If $s$ and $t$ are terms
such that $\Delta$ contains the equation $s = t$ and the formula $\varphi(s)$, then $\Delta$
contains $\varphi(t)$.

articles.title: Lowering a term with no bound variables
articles.statement:
A term whose variables are free variables from
$\mathbb{N}$ together with bound variables from the empty index set is lowered to the term over
$\mathbb{N}$ of the same shape, in which every free variable $x$ stays $x$.

articles.title: Derivations survive language homomorphisms
articles.statement:
Let $h : L \to L'$ be a homomorphism of
first-order languages, and write $h(\varphi)$ for the formula of $L'$ obtained from a formula
$\varphi$ of $L$ by replacing each symbol by its image under $h$. Let $\Gamma$ be a finite list of
formulas of $L$ with free variables in $\alpha$, and let $\varphi$ be a formula of $L$ with free
variables in $\alpha$. If $\Gamma \vdash \varphi$ in natural deduction, then
$h(\Gamma) \vdash h(\varphi)$, where $h(\Gamma)$ is the list of the images of the members of
$\Gamma$.

The calculus never inspects a symbol.

## Sources

- D. van Dalen, *Logic and Structure*, 5th ed., Springer 2013, §3.1.

articles.title: Maximal consistent set
articles.statement:
A set $\Delta$ of formulas is maximal consistent when it is
consistent and every consistent set of formulas containing $\Delta$ is contained in
$\Delta$, that is, equals $\Delta$.

articles.title: The relation symbol of an atomic formula occurs in it
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a first-order
language, $R$ an $l$-ary relation symbol of $L$, and $t_1, \dots, t_l$ $L$-terms with free
variables in $\alpha$ and $n$ bound variables. Then $R$ belongs to the finite set of symbols
occurring in the atomic bounded formula $R(t_1, \dots, t_l)$.

## Sources

- D. van Dalen, *Logic and Structure*, 5th ed., Springer 2013, §3.1.

articles.title: Maximal consistent sets absorb consistent extensions
articles.statement:
Let $\Delta$ be a maximal consistent
set of first-order formulas of a language $L$ with free variables in $\alpha$, and let $\varphi$ be
a formula. If $\Delta \cup \{\varphi\}$ is consistent, then $\varphi \in \Delta$.

articles.title: Maximal consistent sets of first-order formulas are deductively closed
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a
first-order language, let $\alpha$ be an infinite type of variables, and let $\Delta$ be a maximal
consistent set of formulas of $L$ with free variables in $\alpha$. Every formula $\varphi$ that
$\Delta$ proves lies in $\Delta$.

articles.title: Symbols of a generated sublanguage occur in the generating formulas
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a
first-order language and $F$ a finite set of $L$-formulas with free variables in $\mathbb{N}$. The
map from the symbols of the sublanguage of $L$ on the symbols occurring in $F$ to the symbols of
$L$ sends every symbol of that sublanguage to a symbol occurring in some formula of $F$.

## Sources

- H.-D. Ebbinghaus, J. Flum, and W. Thomas, *Mathematical Logic*, 2nd ed., Springer 1994, Chapter V.

articles.title: A symbol of a member of a set of formulas is a symbol of the set
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a first-order
language, $F$ a finite set of $L$-formulas with free variables in $\mathbb{N}$, and $\psi \in F$.
Every symbol occurring in $\psi$ belongs to the finite set of symbols occurring in some formula
of $F$.

## Sources

- D. van Dalen, *Logic and Structure*, 5th ed., Springer 2013, §3.1.

articles.title: The head function symbol of a term occurs in it
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a first-order language, $f$
an $l$-ary function symbol of $L$, and $t_1, \dots, t_l$ $L$-terms with variables in $\alpha$.
Then $f$ belongs to the finite set of symbols occurring in the term $f(t_1, \dots, t_l)$.

## Sources

- D. van Dalen, *Logic and Structure*, 5th ed., Springer 2013, §3.1.

articles.title: Modus ponens for provability from sets
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a first-order language, let $\alpha$ be
an infinite type of variables, and let $S$ be a set of formulas of $L$ with free variables in
$\alpha$. For formulas $\varphi$ and $\psi$, if $S$ proves $\varphi \to \psi$ and $S$ proves
$\varphi$, then $S$ proves $\psi$.

articles.title: Maximal consistent sets decide every formula
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a first-order language, let
$\alpha$ be an infinite type of variables, and let $\Delta$ be a maximal consistent set of formulas
of $L$ with free variables in $\alpha$. For every formula $\varphi$, $\neg\varphi \in \Delta$ if
and only if $\varphi \notin \Delta$; so exactly one of $\varphi$ and $\neg\varphi$ lies in
$\Delta$.

articles.title: Ex falso for provability from sets
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a first-order language, let $\alpha$ be an
infinite type of variables, and let $S$ be a set of formulas of $L$ with free variables in
$\alpha$. If $S$ proves $\bot$, then $S$ proves every formula $\varphi$.

articles.title: Language homomorphisms commute with instantiation in formulas
articles.statement:
Let $h \colon L \to L'$ be
a homomorphism of first-order languages. For an $L$-term or bounded $L$-formula $x$, write $h(x)$
for the term or bounded formula of $L'$ obtained by replacing every symbol by its image under
$h$. Let $t$ be an $L$-term with free variables in $\alpha$ and $\varphi$ a bounded $L$-formula
with free variables in $\alpha$ and $m + 1$ bound variables. Then $h$ applied to the
instantiation of $t$ for the outermost bound variable (the one with index $0$) of $\varphi$
equals the instantiation of $h(t)$ for the outermost bound variable of $h(\varphi)$.

## Sources

- D. van Dalen, *Logic and Structure*, 5th ed., Springer 2013, §3.1.

articles.title: Language homomorphisms preserve equations
articles.statement:
Let $h \colon L \to L'$ be a homomorphism of
first-order languages. For an $L$-term or $L$-formula $x$, write $h(x)$ for the term or formula
of $L'$ obtained by replacing every symbol by its image under $h$. If $s$ and $t$ are $L$-terms
with free variables in $\alpha$, then $h$ applied to the formula $s = t$ is the formula
$h(s) = h(t)$.

## Sources

- D. van Dalen, *Logic and Structure*, 5th ed., Springer 2013, §3.1.

articles.title: Language homomorphisms commute with instantiation in terms
articles.statement:
Let $h \colon L \to L'$ be a
homomorphism of first-order languages, and for an $L$-term $u$ write $h(u)$ for the $L'$-term
obtained by replacing every function symbol by its image under $h$. Let $t$ be an $L$-term with
free variables in $\alpha$ and $s$ an $L$-term with free variables in $\alpha$ and $m + 1$
bound variables. Then $h$ applied to the instantiation of $t$ for the outermost bound variable
(the one with index $0$) of $s$ equals the instantiation of $h(t)$ for the outermost bound
variable of $h(s)$.

## Sources

- D. van Dalen, *Logic and Structure*, 5th ed., Springer 2013, §3.1.

articles.title: Language homomorphisms commute with renaming variables
articles.statement:
Let $h \colon L \to L'$ be a
homomorphism of first-order languages, and for an $L$-term $u$ write $h(u)$ for the $L'$-term
obtained by replacing every function symbol by its image under $h$. Let $t$ be an $L$-term with
variables in $\alpha$ and $g \colon \alpha \to \beta$ a map. Then $h$ applied to the term
obtained from $t$ by renaming each variable $a$ to $g(a)$ equals the term obtained from $h(t)$
by the same renaming.

## Sources

- D. van Dalen, *Logic and Structure*, 5th ed., Springer 2013, §3.1 (derivations depend only on the shape of a formula, not on the names of its symbols).

articles.title: Language homomorphisms commute with substitution in terms
articles.statement:
Let $h \colon L \to L'$ be a
homomorphism of first-order languages, and for an $L$-term $u$ write $h(u)$ for the $L'$-term
obtained by replacing every function symbol by its image under $h$. Let $s$ be an $L$-term with
variables in $\beta$ and $g$ a map assigning to each $b \in \beta$ an $L$-term $g(b)$ with
variables in $\gamma$. Then $h$ applied to the term obtained from $s$ by substituting $g(b)$ for
each variable $b$ equals the term obtained from $h(s)$ by substituting $h(g(b))$ for each
variable $b$.

## Sources

- D. van Dalen, *Logic and Structure*, 5th ed., Springer 2013, §3.1.

articles.title: Soundness and completeness for arbitrary languages
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a first-order language,
with no countability hypothesis, $T$ a theory of $L$ (a set of sentences), and $\varphi$ an
$L$-formula with free variables in $\mathbb{N}$. Then $\varphi$ is provable from the sentences of
$T$, each regarded as a formula with free variables in $\mathbb{N}$, if and only if $\varphi$
holds in every nonempty model of $T$ under every assignment of elements of the model to the
variables in $\mathbb{N}$.

The models range over types in the universe $\max(u, v)$, where $u$ and $v$ are the universe
levels of the function and relation symbols of $L$.

## Sources

- L. Henkin, *The completeness of the first-order functional calculus*, J. Symbolic Logic 14, 1949, 159-166.

articles.title: Soundness and completeness of first-order natural deduction
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a language with
countably many function and relation symbols, whose function symbols live in universe $u$ and
relation symbols in universe $v$. For every theory $T$ of $L$ and every formula $\varphi$ of $L$
with free variables in $\mathbb{N}$, $\varphi$ is provable from the sentences of $T$, viewed as
formulas over $\mathbb{N}$, if and only if $\varphi$ holds under every assignment of the
variables in every nonempty model of $T$ whose carrier lies in universe $\max(u, v)$.

articles.title: Provability as inconsistency with the negation
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a first-order language, let
$\alpha$ be an infinite type of variables, let $S$ be a set of formulas of $L$ with free variables
in $\alpha$, and let $\varphi$ be a formula. Then $S$ proves $\varphi$ if and only if
$S \cup \{\neg\varphi\}$ is not consistent.

articles.title: Refutability as inconsistency
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a first-order language, let $\alpha$ be an
infinite type of variables, let $S$ be a set of formulas of $L$ with free variables in $\alpha$,
and let $\varphi$ be a formula. Then $S$ proves $\neg\varphi$ if and only if
$S \cup \{\varphi\}$ is not consistent.

articles.title: Strong completeness for arbitrary languages
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a first-order language whose
function symbols live in universe $u$ and relation symbols in universe $v$, with no restriction
on the number of symbols. Let $S$ be a set of formulas of $L$ and $\varphi$ a formula of $L$,
all with free variables in $\mathbb{N}$. If for every $L$-structure $M$ with carrier in
universe $\max(u, v)$ and every assignment $e : \mathbb{N} \to M$ under which all formulas of
$S$ hold, $\varphi$ also holds under $e$, then $\varphi$ is provable from $S$.

## Sources

- L. Henkin, *The completeness of the first-order functional calculus*, J. Symbolic Logic 14, 1949, 159-166.

articles.title: Strong completeness of first-order natural deduction
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a language with
countably many function and relation symbols, whose function symbols live in universe $u$. Let
$S$ be a set of formulas of $L$ and $\varphi$ a formula of $L$, all with free variables in
$\mathbb{N}$. If for every $L$-structure $M$ with carrier in universe $u$ and every assignment
$v : \mathbb{N} \to M$ under which all formulas of $S$ hold, $\varphi$ also holds under $v$,
then $\varphi$ is provable from $S$.

articles.title: Completeness for arbitrary languages
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a first-order language whose function
symbols live in universe $u$ and relation symbols in universe $v$, with no restriction on the
number of symbols. Let $T$ be a theory of $L$ and $\varphi$ a formula of $L$ with free
variables in $\mathbb{N}$. If $\varphi$ holds under every assignment of the variables in every
nonempty model of $T$ whose carrier lies in universe $\max(u, v)$, then $\varphi$ is provable
from the sentences of $T$, viewed as formulas over $\mathbb{N}$.

## Sources

- L. Henkin, *The completeness of the first-order functional calculus*, J. Symbolic Logic 14, 1949, 159-166.

articles.title: Completeness of first-order natural deduction for theories
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a language with
countably many function and relation symbols, whose function symbols live in universe $u$ and
relation symbols in universe $v$. Let $T$ be a theory of $L$ and $\varphi$ a formula of $L$ with
free variables in $\mathbb{N}$. If $\varphi$ holds under every assignment of the variables in
every nonempty model of $T$ whose carrier lies in universe $\max(u, v)$, then $\varphi$ is
provable from the sentences of $T$, viewed as formulas over $\mathbb{N}$.

articles.title: Truth lemma for the first-order term model
articles.statement:
Let $\Delta$ be a maximal consistent set of
formulas with free variables in $\mathbb{N}$ such that, for every formula $\varphi$ with one
bound variable, if $\Delta$ contains $\varphi(t)$ for every term $t$ (where $\varphi(t)$ is the
result of substituting $t$ for the bound variable), then $\Delta$ contains $\forall x\,\varphi$.
Then a formula $\psi$ with free variables in $\mathbb{N}$ holds in the term model of $\Delta$
under the canonical assignment $x \mapsto [x]$ if and only if $\psi \in \Delta$.

articles.title: Replacing an argument of a relation symbol by an equal term
articles.statement:
Let $\Delta$ be a maximal
consistent set of formulas with free variables in $\mathbb{N}$, let $R$ be an $n$-ary relation
symbol, let $x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}$, $a$ and $b$ be terms with variables in $\mathbb{N}$, and let
$i < n$. If $\Delta$ contains $a = b$ and contains $R(x_0, \dots, x_{n-1})$ with $x_i$ replaced
by $a$, then $\Delta$ contains $R(x_0, \dots, x_{n-1})$ with $x_i$ replaced by $b$.

articles.title: Doubling the variables preserves consistency
articles.statement:
If $S$ is a consistent set of formulas with
free variables in $\mathbb{N}$, then the set obtained from $S$ by renaming every free variable
$x$ to $2x$ in each of its formulas is consistent.

Halving the variables maps any derivation of $\bot$ from the renamed set back to one from $S$.

articles.title: Renaming free variables along an arbitrary map preserves derivability
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ and
$\beta$ be types of variables with $\beta$ infinite, and let $f : \alpha \to \beta$ be any map.
If $\varphi$ is derivable from the list of hypotheses $\Gamma$ in natural deduction, then the
formula obtained from $\varphi$ by renaming each free variable $x$ to $f(x)$ is derivable from
the list obtained by renaming the free variables of each formula of $\Gamma$ in the same way.

The map need not be injective: in the proof each eigenvariable is sent to a fresh variable.

articles.title: Renaming depends only on the free variables
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be types of
variables, let $n \in \mathbb{N}$, and let $\varphi$ be a formula with free variables in $\alpha$
and $n$ further variables reserved for binding by enclosing quantifiers. If two maps
$f, g : \alpha \to \beta$ agree on every variable from $\alpha$ that occurs free in $\varphi$,
then renaming the variables of $\varphi$ from $\alpha$ along $f$ and along $g$ gives the same
formula.

articles.title: The inclusion of the sublanguage of a finite set of formulas is injective
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a
first-order language. For every finite set $F$ of formulas of $L$ with free variables in
$\mathbb{N}$, the inclusion into $L$ of the sublanguage of $L$ on the symbols occurring in $F$
is injective on function symbols and on relation symbols.

## Sources

- H.-D. Ebbinghaus, J. Flum, and W. Thomas, *Mathematical Logic*, 2nd ed., Springer 1994, Chapter V.

articles.title: Inclusion of the sublanguage of a finite set of formulas
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a first-order
language. For a finite set $F$ of formulas of $L$ with free variables in $\mathbb{N}$, this is
the language homomorphism from the sublanguage of $L$ on the symbols occurring in $F$ into $L$
that sends each function symbol and each relation symbol to itself.

## Sources

- H.-D. Ebbinghaus, J. Flum, and W. Thomas, *Mathematical Logic*, 2nd ed., Springer 1994, Chapter V.

articles.title: Preimage of a finite set of formulas in its sublanguage
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a first-order
language. For a finite set $F$ of formulas of $L$ with free variables in $\mathbb{N}$, this is
the set of those formulas $\psi_0$ of the sublanguage of $L$ on the symbols occurring in $F$,
with free variables in $\mathbb{N}$, whose image under the inclusion of that sublanguage into
$L$ belongs to $F$.

## Sources

- H.-D. Ebbinghaus, J. Flum, and W. Thomas, *Mathematical Logic*, 2nd ed., Springer 1994, Chapter V.

articles.title: The symbol map of the sublanguage of a finite set of formulas is injective
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be
a first-order language. For every finite set $F$ of formulas of $L$ with free variables in
$\mathbb{N}$, the map sending each symbol of the sublanguage of $L$ on the symbols occurring in
$F$ to the same symbol of $L$ is injective.

## Sources

- H.-D. Ebbinghaus, J. Flum, and W. Thomas, *Mathematical Logic*, 2nd ed., Springer 1994, Chapter V.

articles.title: Symbols of the sublanguage of a finite set of formulas as symbols of the language
articles.statement:
Let
$L$ be a first-order language. For a finite set $F$ of formulas of $L$ with free variables in
$\mathbb{N}$, this map sends each function symbol (respectively relation symbol) of the
sublanguage of $L$ on the symbols occurring in $F$ to the same function symbol (respectively
relation symbol) of $L$, with the same arity.

## Sources

- H.-D. Ebbinghaus, J. Flum, and W. Thomas, *Mathematical Logic*, 2nd ed., Springer 1994, Chapter V.

articles.title: Sublanguage of a finite set of formulas
articles.statement:
For a finite set $F$ of formulas of a
first-order language $L$ with free variables in $\mathbb{N}$, the sublanguage of $L$ on the
symbols occurring in $F$ has as its $n$-ary function symbols the $n$-ary function symbols of
$L$ that occur in some formula of $F$, and as its $n$-ary relation symbols the $n$-ary
relation symbols of $L$ that occur in some formula of $F$.

## Sources

- H.-D. Ebbinghaus, J. Flum, and W. Thomas, *Mathematical Logic*, 2nd ed., Springer 1994, Chapter V (the sublanguage generated by a finite set of formulas).

articles.title: Term substitution depends only on the values of the substitution
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a
first-order language, let $s$ be a term of $L$ with variables in a type $\beta$, and let $g$ and
$g'$ assign to each variable in $\beta$ a term of $L$ with variables in a type $\gamma$. If
$g(a) = g'(a)$ for every $a \in \beta$, then substituting $g$ into $s$ gives the same term as
substituting $g'$ into $s$.

## Sources

- D. van Dalen, *Logic and Structure*, 5th ed., Springer 2013, §3.1.

articles.title: Symbols of the sublanguage as symbols occurring in a finite set of formulas
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be
a first-order language. For a finite set $F$ of formulas of $L$ with free variables in
$\mathbb{N}$, this map sends each symbol of the sublanguage of $L$ on the symbols occurring in
$F$ to the same symbol of $L$, regarded as an element of the finite set of symbols occurring in
$F$.

## Sources

- H.-D. Ebbinghaus, J. Flum, and W. Thomas, *Mathematical Logic*, 2nd ed., Springer 1994, Chapter V.

articles.title: Symbols of a finite set of formulas
articles.statement:
For a finite set $F$ of first-order formulas of a
language $L$ with free variables indexed by $\mathbb{N}$, the symbols of $F$ are the finite set
of function and relation symbols of $L$ that occur in some formula of $F$, that is, the union over
$\psi \in F$ of the finite sets of symbols occurring in $\psi$.

## Sources

- D. van Dalen, *Logic and Structure*, 5th ed., Springer 2013, §3.1.

articles.title: Canonical assignment of the term model
articles.statement:
For a maximal consistent set $\Delta$ of formulas
with free variables in $\mathbb{N}$, the canonical assignment sends each variable
$x \in \mathbb{N}$ to $[x]$, the class of the variable term $x$ in the term model of $\Delta$.

articles.title: Term model of a maximal consistent set
articles.statement:
For a maximal consistent set $\Delta$ of formulas
with free variables in $\mathbb{N}$, the term model of $\Delta$ is the set of terms with
variables in $\mathbb{N}$ modulo the equivalence relation that identifies $s$ and $t$ when the
formula $s = t$ belongs to $\Delta$.

articles.title: Provable equality of terms
articles.statement:
Let $\Delta$ be a maximal consistent set of first-order
formulas in a language $L$ with free variables in $\mathbb{N}$. Provable equality in $\Delta$ is
the equivalence relation on $L$-terms with variables in $\mathbb{N}$ under which $s \sim t$ holds
exactly when the equation $s = t$ belongs to $\Delta$.

articles.title: Term structure of a set of formulas
articles.statement:
Let $\Delta$ be a set of first-order formulas in a
language $L$ with free variables in $\mathbb{N}$. The term structure of $\Delta$ is the
$L$-structure whose domain is the set of $L$-terms with variables in $\mathbb{N}$, in which an
$n$-ary function symbol $f$ sends terms $t_1, \dots, t_n$ to the term $f(t_1, \dots, t_n)$, and
an $n$-ary relation symbol $R$ holds of $t_1, \dots, t_n$ exactly when the atomic formula
$R(t_1, \dots, t_n)$ belongs to $\Delta$.

articles.title: Symbols of the left side of an equation
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a first-order language and let $t_1$,
$t_2$ be terms of $L$ in free variables from $\alpha$ and $n$ bound variables. Every symbol
occurring in $t_1$ occurs in the atomic formula $t_1 = t_2$, viewed as a formula with $n$ bound
variables: the finite set of symbols of $t_1$ is contained in that of $t_1 = t_2$.

## Sources

- D. van Dalen, *Logic and Structure*, 5th ed., Springer 2013, §3.1.

articles.title: Symbols of the right side of an equation
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a first-order language and let
$t_1$, $t_2$ be terms of $L$ in free variables from $\alpha$ and $n$ bound variables. Every symbol
occurring in $t_2$ occurs in the atomic formula $t_1 = t_2$, viewed as a formula with $n$ bound
variables: the finite set of symbols of $t_2$ is contained in that of $t_1 = t_2$.

## Sources

- D. van Dalen, *Logic and Structure*, 5th ed., Springer 2013, §3.1.

articles.title: Symbols of an argument of a function application
articles.statement:
Let $f$ be an $l$-ary function symbol
of a first-order language $L$ and let $t_0, \dots, t_{l-1}$ be terms of $L$ in variables from
$\alpha$. For every $i < l$, every symbol occurring in $t_i$ occurs in the term
$f(t_0, \dots, t_{l-1})$: the finite set of symbols of $t_i$ is contained in that of
$f(t_0, \dots, t_{l-1})$.

## Sources

- D. van Dalen, *Logic and Structure*, 5th ed., Springer 2013, §3.1.

articles.title: Symbols of an argument of a relational atomic formula
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be an $l$-ary relation
symbol of a first-order language $L$ and let $t_0, \dots, t_{l-1}$ be terms of $L$ in free
variables from $\alpha$ and $n$ bound variables. For every $i < l$, every symbol occurring in
$t_i$ occurs in the atomic formula $R(t_0, \dots, t_{l-1})$, viewed as a formula with $n$ bound
variables: the finite set of symbols of $t_i$ is contained in that of $R(t_0, \dots, t_{l-1})$.

## Sources

- D. van Dalen, *Logic and Structure*, 5th ed., Springer 2013, §3.1.

articles.title: Finite set of symbols of a term
articles.statement:
The finite set of symbols occurring in a term $t$ of a
first-order language $L$, a finite subset of the function and relation symbols of $L$, is
defined by recursion on $t$: it is empty when $t$ is a variable, and when
$t = f(t_0, \dots, t_{l-1})$ for an $l$-ary function symbol $f$ it consists of $f$ together with
the symbols occurring in each of $t_0, \dots, t_{l-1}$.

## Sources

- D. van Dalen, *Logic and Structure*, 5th ed., Springer 2013, §3.1 (the finite set of symbols occurring in a finite derivation).

articles.title: Replacing arguments one at a time
articles.statement:
Let $r$ be a relation on a type $\beta$, let $n$ be a
natural number and let $P$ be a property of $n$-tuples $x = (x_i)_{i < n}$ in $\beta$. Suppose
that for every tuple $x$, every position $i$ and all $a, b \in \beta$ with $r(a, b)$, if $P$
holds of $x$ with its $i$-th entry replaced by $a$, then $P$ holds of $x$ with its $i$-th entry
replaced by $b$. Then for all tuples $x, y$ with $r(x_i, y_i)$ for every $i$, $P(x)$ implies
$P(y)$.

articles.title: Variable bound of a formula
articles.statement:
Let $\varphi$ be a first-order formula whose variables are
natural numbers together with $n$ variables reserved for quantifiers. Its variable bound
$b(\varphi)$ is one more than the largest natural number occurring as a free variable of
$\varphi$, or $1$ when there is none; it is a strict upper bound on these free variables.

articles.title: Language homomorphisms preserve the free variables of a term
articles.statement:
Let $\phi : L \to L'$ be a
homomorphism of first-order languages and let $t$ be a term of $L$ in free variables from
$\alpha$ and $n$ bound variables. The finite set of free variables from $\alpha$ occurring in the
image $\phi(t)$ of $t$ under $\phi$ equals the finite set of those occurring in $t$.

## Sources

- D. van Dalen, *Logic and Structure*, 5th ed., Springer 2013, §3.1.

articles.title: Witness bases
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a first-order language with countably many symbols, let
$\varphi_0, \varphi_1, \dots$ be the fixed surjective enumeration of the $L$-formulas with free
variables in $\mathbb{N}$ and one variable reserved for a quantifier, and let $b(\varphi)$ be one
more than the largest free variable of $\varphi$, or $1$ if it has none. The witness bases are
defined by $w_0 = b(\varphi_0)$ and $w_{k+1} = w_k + 1 + b(\varphi_{k+1})$. They are strictly
increasing, and $w_k$ exceeds every free variable of $\varphi_0, \dots, \varphi_k$.

articles.title: Henkin witnesses
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a first-order language with countably many symbols and let
$w_0 < w_1 < \dots$ be its witness bases, built from the fixed enumeration
$\varphi_0, \varphi_1, \dots$ of the $L$-formulas with one variable reserved for a quantifier.
The $k$-th Henkin witness is the variable $c_k = 2 w_k + 1$. It is odd, so it is not a free
variable of any formula whose free variables are all even, and it exceeds every free variable
of $\varphi_0, \dots, \varphi_k$.

articles.title: Bisimilar worlds
articles.statement:
Let $M$ and $N$ be Kripke models over the same atoms. A world $w$ of
$M$ and a world $v$ of $N$ are bisimilar if some bisimulation between $M$ and $N$ relates $w$
to $v$.

articles.title: Bisimulation
articles.statement:
Let $M$ and $N$ be Kripke models over the same atoms, with sets of
worlds $W$ and $V$ and accessibility relations $R_M$ and $R_N$. A relation
$Z \subseteq W \times V$ is a bisimulation between $M$ and $N$ when, for all $w \in W$ and
$v \in V$ with $w \mathrel{Z} v$: each atom $a$ is true at $w$ in $M$ if and only if $a$ is
true at $v$ in $N$; for every $w'$ with $w \mathrel{R_M} w'$ there is $v'$ with
$v \mathrel{R_N} v'$ and $w' \mathrel{Z} v'$ (forth); and for every $v'$ with
$v \mathrel{R_N} v'$ there is $w'$ with $w \mathrel{R_M} w'$ and $w' \mathrel{Z} v'$ (back).

articles.title: Bisimilar worlds are modally equivalent
articles.statement:
If a world $w$ of a Kripke model $M$ and a world
$v$ of a Kripke model $N$ over the same atoms are bisimilar, then every modal formula $\varphi$
is satisfied at $w$ in $M$ if and only if $\varphi$ is satisfied at $v$ in $N$.

articles.title: Bisimulations preserve modal formulas
articles.statement:
Let $Z$ be a bisimulation between Kripke models
$M$ and $N$ over the same atoms. If $Z$ relates a world $w$ of $M$ to a world $v$ of $N$, then
every modal formula $\varphi$ is satisfied at $w$ in $M$ if and only if $\varphi$ is satisfied
at $v$ in $N$.

articles.title: Epistemic formulas
articles.statement:
Given a type of atoms and a type of agents, the formulas of epistemic
logic are built inductively: every atom $p$ is a formula, falsity $\bot$ is a formula, if $\varphi$
and $\psi$ are formulas then so is the implication $\varphi \to \psi$, and if $\varphi$ is a
formula and $i$ is an agent then $K_i \varphi$ (read "agent $i$ knows $\varphi$") is a formula.

articles.title: Epistemic models
articles.statement:
Given a type of worlds $W$, a type of atoms and a type of agents, an
epistemic model consists of a binary accessibility relation $R_i$ on $W$ for each agent $i$ and a
valuation assigning to each world the atoms true there; the world type $W$ is required to be
nonempty.

Nonemptiness is assumed as for Kripke models: with no worlds, validity would hold vacuously and
even $\bot$ would be valid.

articles.title: Agent 1 knows that agent 0 knows whether the coin is heads
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be the atom "the coin
is heads" of the two-agent coin model. At every world of that model the formula
$K_1(K_0 p \lor K_0 \neg p)$ holds: agent $1$ knows that agent $0$ either knows $p$ or knows
$\neg p$.

articles.title: Agent 1 does not know that the coin is heads
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be the atom "the coin is heads" of
the two-agent coin model. The formula $K_1 p$ is false at the heads world: agent $1$ considers
the tails world possible.

articles.title: The two-agent coin model
articles.statement:
The epistemic model whose worlds are the two booleans, with
$\mathrm{true}$ read as heads and $\mathrm{false}$ as tails, with a single atom $p$ true exactly
at the heads world, and with two agents $0$ and $1$: agent $0$ sees the coin, so its
accessibility relation is equality of worlds, and agent $1$ does not, so its accessibility
relation relates every pair of worlds.

articles.title: Falsity is not valid in an epistemic model
articles.statement:
In every epistemic model, the formula $\bot$
is not valid: it fails at some world.

The nonempty world set rules out vacuous validity.

articles.title: Negation of epistemic formulas
articles.statement:
The negation $\neg\varphi$ of an epistemic formula
$\varphi$ is the implication $\varphi \to \bot$.

articles.title: Disjunction of epistemic formulas
articles.statement:
The disjunction $\varphi \lor \psi$ of epistemic
formulas $\varphi$ and $\psi$ is the implication $\neg\varphi \to \psi$.

articles.title: Agent 0 knows the coin is heads exactly at heads
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be the atom "the coin is heads"
of the two-agent coin model. At a world $v$ of that model, the formula $K_0 p$ holds if and only
if $v$ is the heads world: agent $0$ sees the coin.

articles.title: Agent 0 knows the coin is tails exactly at tails
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be the atom "the coin is heads"
of the two-agent coin model. At a world $v$ of that model, the formula $K_0 \neg p$ holds if and
only if $v$ is the tails world.

articles.title: Satisfaction of a disjunction
articles.statement:
In an epistemic model $M$, the disjunction
$\varphi \lor \psi$ of two formulas, defined as $\neg \varphi \to \psi$, is satisfied at a world
$w$ if and only if $\varphi$ is satisfied at $w$ or $\psi$ is satisfied at $w$.

articles.title: Satisfaction in an epistemic model
articles.statement:
Satisfaction of an epistemic formula at a world $w$
of a model $M$ is defined by recursion on the formula, writing $R_i$ for the accessibility
relation of agent $i$ in $M$ and $K_i \varphi$ for the formula "agent $i$ knows $\varphi$": an
atom $a$ holds at $w$ when the valuation of $M$ makes $a$ true at $w$; $\bot$ holds at no world;
$\varphi \to \psi$ holds at $w$ when $\psi$ holds at $w$ whenever $\varphi$ does; and
$K_i \varphi$ holds at $w$ when $\varphi$ holds at every world $v$ with $w \mathrel{R_i} v$.

articles.title: Distribution axiom K
articles.statement:
Write $K_i \varphi$ for "agent $i$ knows $\varphi$". For every
epistemic model $M$, every agent $i$ and all formulas $\varphi$ and $\psi$, the formula
$K_i (\varphi \to \psi) \to (K_i \varphi \to K_i \psi)$ is valid in $M$: knowledge distributes
over implication.

articles.title: Negative introspection axiom 5
articles.statement:
Write $K_i \varphi$ for "agent $i$ knows $\varphi$".
Let $M$ be an epistemic model in which the accessibility relation $R_i$ of agent $i$ is
euclidean: for all worlds $a$, $b$, $c$, if $a \mathrel{R_i} b$ and $a \mathrel{R_i} c$ then
$b \mathrel{R_i} c$. Then for every formula $\varphi$, the formula
$\neg K_i \varphi \to K_i \neg K_i \varphi$ is valid in $M$.

articles.title: Positive introspection axiom 4
articles.statement:
Write $K_i \varphi$ for "agent $i$ knows $\varphi$".
Let $M$ be an epistemic model in which the accessibility relation $R_i$ of agent $i$ is
transitive. Then for every formula $\varphi$, the formula $K_i \varphi \to K_i K_i \varphi$ is
valid in $M$.

articles.title: Truth axiom T
articles.statement:
Write $K_i \varphi$ for "agent $i$ knows $\varphi$". Let $M$ be an
epistemic model in which the accessibility relation $R_i$ of agent $i$ is reflexive. Then for
every formula $\varphi$, the formula $K_i \varphi \to \varphi$ is valid in $M$.

articles.title: Validity in an epistemic model
articles.statement:
A formula $\varphi$ is valid in an epistemic model $M$
when $\varphi$ is satisfied at every world of $M$.

articles.title: Finite-check criterion for K-theorems
articles.statement:
A modal formula $\varphi$ is a theorem of K iff it
passes the following finite check: for every nonempty set $U$ of subsets of the set
$\mathrm{sub}(\varphi)$ of subformulas of $\varphi$, every relation $R \subseteq U \times U$ and
every $s \in U$, $\varphi$ evaluates to true at $s$ in the finite Kripke model on $U$ with
relation $R$ in which an atom $p$ is true at $s$ iff $p \in s$.

articles.title: K-theorems via finite models on sets of subformulas
articles.statement:
A modal formula $\varphi$ is a theorem
of K iff for every nonempty set $U$ of subsets of the set $\mathrm{sub}(\varphi)$ of subformulas of
$\varphi$ and every finite set $R$ of pairs of finite sets of formulas, $\varphi$ holds at every
world of the Kripke model whose worlds are the elements of $U$, in which $s$ sees $t$ iff
$(s, t) \in R$, and in which an atom $p$ is true at $s$ iff $p \in s$.

articles.title: S4-provability via finite reflexive transitive models
articles.statement:
A modal formula $\varphi$ is a
theorem of S4 if and only if, for every nonempty set $U$ of subsets of $\mathrm{sub}(\varphi)$,
the set of subformulas of $\varphi$, and every relation $R \subseteq U \times U$ that is reflexive
and transitive on $U$, the formula $\varphi$ is true at every world $s \in U$ of the finite model
with worlds $U$, accessibility relation $R$, and each atom true at $s$ exactly when it belongs
to $s$.

articles.title: S5-provability via finite equivalence models
articles.statement:
A modal formula $\varphi$ is a theorem of
S5 if and only if, for every nonempty set $U$ of subsets of $\mathrm{sub}(\varphi)$, the set of
subformulas of $\varphi$, and every relation $R \subseteq U \times U$ that is reflexive, symmetric
and transitive on $U$, the formula $\varphi$ is true at every world $s \in U$ of the finite model
with worlds $U$, accessibility relation $R$, and each atom true at $s$ exactly when it belongs
to $s$.

articles.title: T-provability via finite reflexive models
articles.statement:
A modal formula $\varphi$ is a theorem of T
if and only if, for every nonempty set $U$ of subsets of $\mathrm{sub}(\varphi)$, the set of
subformulas of $\varphi$, and every relation $R \subseteq U \times U$ that is reflexive on $U$,
the formula $\varphi$ is true at every world $s \in U$ of the finite model with worlds $U$,
accessibility relation $R$, and each atom true at $s$ exactly when it belongs to $s$.

articles.title: Boolean evaluation in a finite model
articles.statement:
Given a finite set $U$ of finite sets of formulas, a
finite set $R$ of pairs of such sets and a finite set $s$ of formulas, the Boolean value of a
formula at $s$ is defined by recursion on the formula: an atom $p$ is true iff $p \in s$; $\bot$ is
false; $\varphi \to \psi$ is true iff $\varphi$ is false or $\psi$ is true at $s$; and $\Box\varphi$
is true iff $\varphi$ is true at every $t \in U$ with $(s, t) \in R$.

For $s \in U$ this computes satisfaction at $s$ in the finite Kripke model on $U$ with relation
$R$ in which an atom is true at a world iff it belongs to it.

articles.title: Finite model property of S4
articles.statement:
If a modal formula $\varphi$ is not a theorem of S4, then
there is a Kripke model with finitely many worlds, at most $2^{|\mathrm{sub}(\varphi)|}$ of them,
where $\mathrm{sub}(\varphi)$ is the set of subformulas of $\varphi$, whose accessibility
relation is reflexive and transitive and in which $\varphi$ is false at some world.

articles.title: Finite model property of S5
articles.statement:
If a modal formula $\varphi$ is not a theorem of S5, then
there is a Kripke model with finitely many worlds, at most $2^{|\mathrm{sub}(\varphi)|}$ of them,
where $\mathrm{sub}(\varphi)$ is the set of subformulas of $\varphi$, whose accessibility
relation is an equivalence relation and in which $\varphi$ is false at some world.

articles.title: Finite model property of T
articles.statement:
If a modal formula $\varphi$ is not a theorem of T, then
there is a Kripke model with finitely many worlds, at most $2^{|\mathrm{sub}(\varphi)|}$ of them,
where $\mathrm{sub}(\varphi)$ is the set of subformulas of $\varphi$, whose accessibility
relation is reflexive and in which $\varphi$ is false at some world.

articles.title: Finite model property of K
articles.statement:
A formula that is not a K-theorem fails in a Kripke model with
at most `2 ^ |sub φ|` worlds.

articles.title: Completeness of K, countermodel form
articles.statement:
A modal formula that is not a theorem of K fails at
some world of some Kripke model.

articles.title: Filtration worlds are realized types
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Kripke model and $\varphi$ a modal
formula, and call the set of subformulas of $\varphi$ satisfied at a world $w$ of $M$ the type of
$w$. Every world $s$ of the filtration of $M$ through the subformulas of $\varphi$, that is, every
element of the finite set of types occurring in $M$, is the type of some world of $M$.

articles.title: Smallest filtration relation
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Kripke model and $\varphi$ a modal formula, and
call the set of subformulas of $\varphi$ satisfied at a world $w$ of $M$ the type of $w$. The
smallest filtration relation is the finite set of pairs $(s, t)$ of types such that there are
worlds $w$ and $w'$ of $M$ of types $s$ and $t$ with $w'$ accessible from $w$.

articles.title: Worlds of the filtration
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Kripke model and $\varphi$ a modal formula. The
worlds of the filtration of $M$ through the subformulas of $\varphi$ form the finite set of types
occurring in $M$: the subsets $s$ of the set $\mathrm{sub}(\varphi)$ of subformulas of $\varphi$
such that $s$ is the set of subformulas of $\varphi$ satisfied at some world of $M$.

articles.title: Smallest filtration of a Kripke model
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Kripke model and $\varphi$ a modal
formula, and call the set of subformulas of $\varphi$ satisfied at a world $w$ of $M$ the type of
$w$. The filtration of $M$ through the subformulas of $\varphi$ is the Kripke model whose worlds
