are the types occurring in $M$, in which a type $s$ sees a type $t$ iff some world of type $s$
sees some world of type $t$ in $M$, and in which an atom $p$ is true at $s$ iff $p \in s$.

articles.title: Finite Kripke model on sets of formulas
articles.statement:
Let $U$ be a nonempty finite set of finite sets of
formulas and $R$ a finite set of pairs of finite sets of formulas. The Kripke model on $U$ with
relation $R$ has the elements of $U$ as worlds, a world $s$ sees a world $t$ iff $(s, t) \in R$,
and an atom $p$ is true at $s$ iff $p \in s$.

articles.title: Filtrations of reflexive models are reflexive
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Kripke model whose
accessibility relation is reflexive, let $\varphi$ be a modal formula, and let $R$ be a
filtration of $M$ through the subformulas of $\varphi$. Then $(s, s) \in R$ for every set $s$
that is the set of subformulas of $\varphi$ true at some world of $M$.

articles.title: Reflexivity on a finite set of worlds
articles.statement:
Let $U$ be a finite set of finite sets of modal
formulas and $R$ a finite set of pairs of such sets. Then $R$ is reflexive on $U$ when
$(s, s) \in R$ for every $s \in U$.

articles.title: Symmetry on a finite set of worlds
articles.statement:
Let $U$ be a finite set of finite sets of modal
formulas and $R$ a finite set of pairs of such sets. Then $R$ is symmetric on $U$ when
$(t, s) \in R$ for all $s, t \in U$ with $(s, t) \in R$.

articles.title: Transitivity on a finite set of worlds
articles.statement:
Let $U$ be a finite set of finite sets of modal
formulas and $R$ a finite set of pairs of such sets. Then $R$ is transitive on $U$ when
$(s, r) \in R$ for all $s, t, r \in U$ with $(s, t) \in R$ and $(t, r) \in R$.

articles.title: The finite check covers the filtration worlds
articles.statement:
Let $C$ be a condition on pairs $(U, R)$ of
a finite set $U$ of sets of formulas and a finite relation $R$ on such sets, and let $\varphi$ be
a formula that passes the finite check for $C$. Let $M$ be a Kripke model, let $U_\varphi$ be the
set of types of worlds of $M$ (the sets of subformulas of $\varphi$ satisfied at a world), and
let $R \subseteq U_\varphi \times U_\varphi$ satisfy $C(U_\varphi, R)$. Then $\varphi$ is valid in
the finite model on $U_\varphi$ with relation $R$, in which an atom holds at $s$ iff it belongs to
$s$.

articles.title: Finite validity check for a frame condition
articles.statement:
Given a condition $C$ on pairs $(U, R)$ of a
finite set $U$ of sets of formulas and a finite set $R$ of pairs of such sets, a formula $\varphi$
passes the finite check for $C$ when, for every nonempty set $U$ of subsets of the subformulas of
$\varphi$ and every relation $R \subseteq U \times U$ with $C(U, R)$, $\varphi$ holds at every
$s \in U$ in the Kripke model with worlds $U$, accessibility relation $R$, and an atom true at
$s$ iff it belongs to $s$.

articles.title: Finite validity check for K
articles.statement:
A modal formula $\varphi$ passes the finite check when,
for every nonempty set $U$ of subsets of the set $\mathrm{sub}(\varphi)$ of subformulas of
$\varphi$, every relation $R \subseteq U \times U$ and every $s \in U$, the formula $\varphi$
is true at $s$ in the Kripke model with set of worlds $U$, accessibility relation $R$, and an
atom $p$ true at a world $t$ iff $p \in t$; truth is computed by recursion on $\varphi$.

articles.title: The smallest filtration is a filtration
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Kripke model and $\varphi$ a modal
formula, and call the set of subformulas of $\varphi$ true at a world $w$ the type of $w$. The
relation that relates two types when some worlds of those types are related in $M$ is a
filtration of $M$ through the set of subformulas of $\varphi$.

articles.title: The Lemmon relation is a filtration of a transitive model
articles.statement:
For every Kripke model $M$
with a transitive accessibility relation and every formula $\varphi$, the Lemmon relation of $M$
and $\varphi$ is a filtration of $M$ through the subformulas of $\varphi$.

articles.title: The S5 relation is a filtration of an equivalence model
articles.statement:
For every Kripke model $M$ whose
accessibility relation is an equivalence relation and every formula $\varphi$, the S5 relation of
$M$ and $\varphi$ is a filtration of $M$ through the subformulas of $\varphi$.

articles.title: Filtration relations
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Kripke model, $\varphi$ a modal formula, $\Sigma$ the
set of subformulas of $\varphi$, and for a world $w$ let $[w]$, the type of $w$, be the set of
formulas of $\Sigma$ true at $w$ in $M$. A relation $R$ on finite sets of formulas is a
filtration of $M$ through $\Sigma$ when (min) for all worlds $w, v$ related in $M$, the pair
$([w], [v])$ is in $R$, and (max) for all worlds $w, v$ with $([w], [v]) \in R$ and every
formula $\psi$ with $\Box\psi \in \Sigma$, if $\Box\psi$ holds at $w$ in $M$ then $\psi$ holds at
$v$ in $M$.

These are conditions (ii) and (iii) of Blackburn–de Rijke–Venema, Definition 2.36, in $\Box$
form; conditions (i) and (iv) (worlds are the $\Sigma$-types, atoms of $\Sigma$ true where they
belong) are built into the construction of the finite model.

articles.title: Lemmon filtration relation
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Kripke model and $\varphi$ a formula, and let
$U_\varphi$ be the set of types of worlds of $M$ (the sets of subformulas of $\varphi$ satisfied at
a world). The Lemmon relation is the relation $R$ on $U_\varphi$ such that $s \mathrel{R} t$ iff
for every formula $\psi$ with $\Box\psi$ a subformula of $\varphi$, $\Box\psi \in s$ implies
$\Box\psi \in t$ and $\psi \in t$.

This is the $\Box$ form of Blackburn–de Rijke–Venema's transitive filtration $R^t$ (Lemma 2.42).

articles.title: A filtration refutes what the model refutes
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Kripke model, $\varphi$ a
formula and $R$ a filtration of $M$ through the subformulas of $\varphi$. If $\varphi$ fails at
some world of $M$, then $\varphi$ is not valid in the finite model whose worlds are the types of
worlds of $M$ (the sets of subformulas of $\varphi$ satisfied at a world), with relation $R$ and
an atom true at a type iff it belongs to it.

articles.title: S5 filtration relation
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Kripke model and $\varphi$ a formula, and let
$U_\varphi$ be the set of types of worlds of $M$ (the sets of subformulas of $\varphi$ satisfied at
a world). The S5 relation is the relation $R$ on $U_\varphi$ such that $s \mathrel{R} t$ iff for
every formula $\psi$ with $\Box\psi$ a subformula of $\varphi$, $\Box\psi \in s$ iff
$\Box\psi \in t$.

articles.title: Filtration lemma for the smallest filtration
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Kripke model, $\varphi$ a
modal formula, and for a world $w$ let $[w]$, the type of $w$, be the set of subformulas of
$\varphi$ true at $w$ in $M$. For every subformula $\psi$ of $\varphi$ and every world $w$ of $M$,
$\psi$ holds at $[w]$ in the smallest filtration of $M$ through the subformulas of $\varphi$ iff
$\psi$ holds at $w$ in $M$.

articles.title: Filtration lemma
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Kripke model, $\varphi$ a modal formula, and for a world
$w$ let $[w]$, the type of $w$, be the set of subformulas of $\varphi$ true at $w$ in $M$. Let $R$
be a filtration of $M$ through the subformulas of $\varphi$, and let $M^R$ be the Kripke model
whose worlds are the types of the worlds of $M$, with accessibility relation $R$ and an atom
true at a type iff the type contains it. Then for every subformula $\psi$ of $\varphi$ and every
world $w$ of $M$, $\psi$ holds at $[w]$ in $M^R$ iff $\psi$ holds at $w$ in $M$.

articles.title: Worlds of the same type agree on subformulas
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Kripke model and $\varphi$ a
modal formula, and call the set of subformulas of $\varphi$ true at a world $w$ of $M$ the type
of $w$. If two worlds $w$ and $v$ of $M$ have the same type, then every subformula $\psi$ of
$\varphi$ holds at $w$ iff it holds at $v$.

articles.title: The subformula relation is transitive
articles.statement:
If $\psi$ is a subformula of a modal formula
$\varphi$, then every subformula of $\psi$ is a subformula of $\varphi$.

articles.title: Type of a world
articles.statement:
Given a Kripke model $M$ and a modal formula $\varphi$, the type (or
$\Sigma$-type, for $\Sigma$ the set of subformulas of $\varphi$) of a world $w$ of $M$ is the
finite set of subformulas of $\varphi$ that hold at $w$ in $M$.

articles.title: Subformulas
articles.statement:
The finite set $\mathrm{sub}(\varphi)$ of subformulas of a modal formula
$\varphi$, including $\varphi$ itself, is defined by recursion: $\mathrm{sub}(p) = \{p\}$ for an
atom $p$, $\mathrm{sub}(\bot) = \{\bot\}$, $\mathrm{sub}(\varphi \to \psi) = \{\varphi \to \psi\}
\cup \mathrm{sub}(\varphi) \cup \mathrm{sub}(\psi)$, and $\mathrm{sub}(\Box\varphi) =
\{\Box\varphi\} \cup \mathrm{sub}(\varphi)$.

articles.title: Conjunction
articles.statement:
For modal formulas $\varphi$ and $\psi$, the conjunction $\varphi \wedge \psi$
is the formula $
eg(\varphi 	o 
eg\psi)$, where $
eg\chi$ stands for $\chi 	o  ot$.

articles.title: Axiom B
articles.statement:
For a modal formula $\varphi$, the symmetry axiom B is the formula
$\varphi 	o \Box\Diamond\varphi$, where $\Diamond\psi$ is $
eg\Box
eg\psi$ and $
eg\chi$ stands
for $\chi 	o  ot$.

articles.title: Axiom D
articles.statement:
For a modal formula $\varphi$, the seriality axiom D is the formula
$\Box\varphi 	o \Diamond\varphi$, where $\Diamond\psi$ is $
eg\Box
eg\psi$ and $
eg\chi$ stands
for $\chi 	o  ot$.

articles.title: Axiom 5
articles.statement:
For a modal formula $\varphi$, the euclidean axiom 5 is the formula
$\Diamond\varphi 	o \Box\Diamond\varphi$, where $\Diamond\psi$ is $
eg\Box
eg\psi$ and $
eg\chi$
stands for $\chi 	o  ot$.

articles.title: Axiom 4
articles.statement:
For a modal formula $\varphi$, the transitivity axiom 4 is the formula
$\Box\varphi \to \Box\Box\varphi$.

articles.title: Axiom K
articles.statement:
For modal formulas $\varphi$ and $\psi$, the distribution axiom K is the formula
$\Box(\varphi \to \psi) \to (\Box\varphi \to \Box\psi)$.

articles.title: Axiom T
articles.statement:
For a modal formula $\varphi$, the reflexivity axiom T is the formula
$\Box\varphi \to \varphi$.

articles.title: Bounded morphism
articles.statement:
Let $M$ and $N$ be Kripke models over the same atoms, with sets of worlds
$W$ and $V$ and accessibility relations $R_M$ and $R_N$. A bounded morphism from $M$ to $N$ is
a map $f : W \to V$ such that every atom holds at a world $w$ in $M$ if and only if it holds
at $f(w)$ in $N$; whenever $w \mathrel{R_M} w'$, also $f(w) \mathrel{R_N} f(w')$ (forth); and
whenever $f(w) \mathrel{R_N} v'$, there is a world $w'$ with $w \mathrel{R_M} w'$ and
$f(w') = v'$ (back).

Bounded morphisms are also called p-morphisms.

articles.title: Composition of bounded morphisms
articles.statement:
Let $M_1$, $M_2$, $M_3$ be Kripke models over the same
atoms. If $f$ is a bounded morphism from $M_1$ to $M_2$ and $g$ is a bounded morphism from $M_2$
to $M_3$, then the composite map $g \circ f$ on worlds is a bounded morphism from $M_1$ to
$M_3$.

articles.title: The possibility operator
articles.statement:
For a modal formula $\varphi$, the formula $\Diamond\varphi$
("possibly $\varphi$") is $
eg\Box
eg\varphi$, where $
eg\chi$ stands for $\chi 	o  ot$.

articles.title: Extensionality for bounded morphisms
articles.statement:
Two bounded morphisms $f$ and $g$ between the same
Kripke models are equal if $f(w) = g(w)$ for every world $w$.

articles.title: Modal formulas
articles.statement:
For a type $\alpha$ of atoms, the formulas of basic modal logic over
$\alpha$ are generated as follows: every atom $p \in \alpha$ is a formula; falsity $\bot$ is a
formula; if $\varphi$ and $\psi$ are formulas then so is the implication $\varphi \to \psi$; and
if $\varphi$ is a formula then so is the necessity formula $\Box\varphi$.

articles.title: Identity bounded morphism
articles.statement:
For every Kripke model $M$, the identity map on the worlds of
$M$ is a bounded morphism from $M$ to itself.

articles.title: Kripke model
articles.statement:
A Kripke model consists of a nonempty collection of worlds, an accessibility relation,
and an atom valuation.

articles.title: Negation of modal formulas
articles.statement:
The negation of a modal formula $\varphi$ is the formula
$\neg\varphi := \varphi \to \bot$.

articles.title: Falsity is valid in no Kripke model
articles.statement:
For every Kripke model $M$, the formula $\bot$ is
not valid in $M$: since $M$ has at least one world and no world satisfies $\bot$, some world
of $M$ fails to satisfy $\bot$.

articles.title: Disjunction of modal formulas
articles.statement:
The disjunction of modal formulas $\varphi$ and $\psi$ is
the formula $\varphi \lor \psi := \neg\varphi \to \psi$, where $\neg\varphi$ is
$\varphi \to \bot$.

articles.title: Semantics of possibility
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Kripke model with accessibility relation $R$, and
let $\Diamond\varphi$ denote the formula $\neg\Box\neg\varphi$, where $\neg\chi$ is
$\chi \to \bot$. For every world $w$ and modal formula $\varphi$, $w$ satisfies $\Diamond\varphi$
in $M$ if and only if there is a world $v$ with $w \mathrel{R} v$ such that $v$ satisfies
$\varphi$ in $M$.

articles.title: Invariance of modal satisfaction under bounded morphisms
articles.statement:
Let $f$ be a bounded morphism
from a Kripke model $M$ to a Kripke model $N$ over the same atoms. Then for every modal formula
$\varphi$ and every world $w$ of $M$, $w$ satisfies $\varphi$ in $M$ if and only if $f(w)$
satisfies $\varphi$ in $N$.

articles.title: Satisfaction in a Kripke model
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Kripke model with accessibility relation
$R$. Satisfaction of a modal formula at a world $w$ of $M$ is defined by recursion on the
formula: $w$ satisfies an atom $p$ if and only if the valuation of $M$ makes $p$ true at $w$;
$w$ never satisfies $\bot$; $w$ satisfies $\varphi \to \psi$ if and only if $w$ satisfies
$\psi$ whenever it satisfies $\varphi$; and $w$ satisfies $\Box\varphi$ if and only if every
world $v$ with $w \mathrel{R} v$ satisfies $\varphi$.

articles.title: The truth constant
articles.statement:
The formula $\top$ is the negation $\neg\bot$ of falsity, that is,
the implication $\bot \to \bot$.

articles.title: Axiom B is valid on symmetric Kripke models
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Kripke model whose
accessibility relation $R$ is symmetric: $R\,u\,v$ implies $R\,v\,u$ for all worlds $u, v$.
Then for every formula $\varphi$ the B axiom $\varphi \to \Box\Diamond\varphi$, where
$\Diamond\varphi$ abbreviates $\neg\Box\neg\varphi$, is globally valid in $M$.

articles.title: Axiom D is valid on serial Kripke models
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Kripke model whose accessibility
relation $R$ is serial: every world $w$ has some world $v$ with $R\,w\,v$. Then for every formula
$\varphi$ the D axiom $\Box\varphi \to \Diamond\varphi$, where $\Diamond\varphi$ abbreviates
$\neg\Box\neg\varphi$, is globally valid in $M$.

articles.title: Axiom 5 is valid on euclidean Kripke models
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Kripke model whose
accessibility relation $R$ is euclidean: $R\,u\,v$ and $R\,u\,w$ imply $R\,v\,w$ for all worlds
$u, v, w$. Then for every formula $\varphi$ the 5 axiom $\Diamond\varphi \to \Box\Diamond\varphi$,
where $\Diamond\varphi$ abbreviates $\neg\Box\neg\varphi$, is globally valid in $M$.

articles.title: Axiom 4 is valid on transitive Kripke models
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Kripke model whose
accessibility relation $R$ is transitive: $R\,u\,v$ and $R\,v\,w$ imply $R\,u\,w$ for all worlds
$u, v, w$. Then for every formula $\varphi$ the 4 axiom $\Box\varphi \to \Box\Box\varphi$ is
globally valid in $M$.

articles.title: Validity of axiom K on Kripke models
articles.statement: The K axiom is valid on every Kripke model.

articles.title: Axiom T is valid on reflexive Kripke models
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Kripke model whose
accessibility relation $R$ is reflexive: $R\,w\,w$ for every world $w$. Then for every formula
$\varphi$ the T axiom $\Box\varphi \to \varphi$ is globally valid in $M$.

articles.title: Surjective bounded morphisms preserve and reflect validity
articles.statement:
Let $M$ and $N$ be Kripke
models over the same atoms and let $f$ be a bounded morphism from $M$ to $N$ whose map on worlds
is surjective. Then for every formula $\varphi$, $\varphi$ is globally valid in $M$ if and only
if $\varphi$ is globally valid in $N$.

articles.title: Global validity in a Kripke model
articles.statement:
A formula $\varphi$ is globally valid in a Kripke
model $M$ when $\varphi$ is satisfied at every world of $M$.

articles.title: $\mathsf{AG}$ is universal reachability
articles.statement:
For every Kripke model $M$, every environment
$\rho$ (an assignment of a predicate on worlds to each variable index), every atom $p$ and every
world $w$, the μ-calculus formula $\mathsf{AG}\,p$ holds at $w$ in $\rho$ if and only if $p$ is
true at every world reachable from $w$ in zero or more steps of the accessibility relation of
$M$.

articles.title: The μ-calculus formula $\mathsf{AG}\,p$
articles.statement:
For an atom $p$, $\mathsf{AG}\,p$ is the
greatest fixed point formula $\nu X.\,(p \wedge \Box X)$. It expresses that every state reachable
from the current one satisfies $p$.

articles.title: μ-calculus formula closed at a given binding depth
articles.statement:
A formula is closed at depth `d` when every free de Bruijn variable is `< d`:
only `μ` / `ν` increase the depth; `□` / `◇` do not bind variables and preserve it.

articles.title: Closed modal μ-calculus formula
articles.statement: A formula is closed when it is closed at depth `0`: every variable is bound.

articles.title: Double complement of a predicate
articles.statement:
For every predicate $S$ on worlds, the predicate
$w \mapsto \neg\neg S(w)$ equals $S$.

articles.title: Depth of a μ-calculus formula is at most its number code
articles.statement:
A formula's depth is at most its code: pairing dominates each component
(`Nat.add_le_pair`).

articles.title: Depth of a modal μ-calculus formula
articles.statement:
The depth of a formula: the length of its longest root-to-leaf path, counting
each connective once.

articles.title: $\mathsf{EF}$ is reachability
articles.statement:
For every Kripke model $M$, every environment $\rho$ (an
assignment of a predicate on worlds to each variable index), every atom $p$ and every world $w$,
the μ-calculus formula $\mathsf{EF}\,p$ holds at $w$ in $\rho$ if and only if $p$ is true at some
world reachable from $w$ in zero or more steps of the accessibility relation of $M$.

articles.title: The μ-calculus formula $\mathsf{EF}\,p$
articles.statement:
For an atom $p$, $\mathsf{EF}\,p$ is the least
fixed point formula $\mu X.\,(p \vee \Diamond X)$. It expresses that some state reachable from
the current one satisfies $p$.

articles.title: Complementing an extended environment
articles.statement:
For every environment $\rho$ (assigning to each
variable index $n$ a predicate $\rho(n)$ on worlds) and every predicate $S$ on worlds,
complementing every predicate of the extension of $\rho$ by $S$ gives the extension of the
complemented environment $n \mapsto \neg\rho(n)$ by the predicate $w \mapsto \neg S(w)$.

articles.title: Extending an environment under a binder
articles.statement:
An environment $\rho$ assigns to each variable
index $n \in \mathbb{N}$ a predicate $\rho(n)$ on worlds. Its extension by a predicate $S$ on
worlds is the environment that assigns $S$ to index $0$ and $\rho(n)$ to index $n + 1$.

With de Bruijn indices, variable $1$ inside a binder thus refers to the enclosing binder.

articles.title: Injectivity of the μ-calculus number code
articles.statement: The encoding is injective.

articles.title: Cantor-pairing number code of a μ-calculus formula
articles.statement:
An injective encoding of μ-calculus formulas over `ℕ` atoms as natural numbers,
via the Cantor pairing function `Nat.pair`. This is a Nat code only, not a complexity
input encoding: repeated pairing squares the code at every unary connective, so the
binary length of the code of `box^d (atom 0)` doubles at each `box` and is exponential
in `d`. Complexity statements use `muTokens` / `muDecodeList` instead.

articles.title: Fuelled decoding inverts the μ-calculus number code
articles.statement:
Decoding inverts encoding, with enough fuel: a formula's own code carries
more fuel than its depth needs.

articles.title: Fuelled decoding of a μ-calculus number code
articles.statement:
Fuelled decoding of a `muCode` number back to a formula. The fuel bounds the
recursion depth; `muDecode` supplies fuel `c + 1`, which exceeds every formula's
depth (see `depth_le_code`).

articles.title: Token-list decoding inverts modal μ-calculus token encoding
articles.statement: Decoding inverts token encoding.

articles.title: Decoding a modal μ-calculus token list to a formula
articles.statement:
Decode a `muTokens` token list back to the formula it encodes, rejecting
trailing tokens.

articles.title: Decoding inverts the μ-calculus number code
articles.statement: Decoding inverts encoding.

articles.title: Decoding a μ-calculus number code to a formula
articles.statement: Decode a `muCode` number back to the formula it encodes.

articles.title: Formulas of the modal μ-calculus
articles.statement:
The formulas over a type of atoms are built from
atoms $a$, negated atoms $\neg a$, variables $X_n$ for $n \in \mathbb{N}$ (de Bruijn indices for
the fixed-point binders), $\bot$ and $\top$ by conjunction $\varphi \wedge \psi$, disjunction
$\varphi \vee \psi$, the modalities $\Box\varphi$ and $\Diamond\varphi$, and the fixed-point
binders $\mu\varphi$ and $\nu\varphi$.

There is no negation of arbitrary formulas. Negated atoms are present so that the meta-level
negation, which swaps each connective with its dual, is an involution.

articles.title: Park induction
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Kripke model, $\rho$ an environment, $\varphi$ a μ-calculus
formula and $P$ a predicate on worlds. If every world satisfying $\varphi$ in the extension of
$\rho$ by $P$ satisfies $P$, then every world satisfying $\mu\varphi$ in $\rho$ satisfies $P$.

articles.title: The least fixed point is contained in its unfolding
articles.statement:
For every Kripke model $M$,
environment $\rho$ and μ-calculus formula $\varphi$, every world satisfying $\mu\varphi$ in $\rho$
also satisfies $\varphi$ in the extension of $\rho$ by the set of worlds satisfying $\mu\varphi$
in $\rho$.

articles.title: The formula $\mu X.\, \mu Y.\, X$ is false everywhere
articles.statement:
For every Kripke model $M$ and
every environment $\rho$, the formula $\mu X.\, \mu Y.\, X$ holds at no world of $M$ under $\rho$.
In de Bruijn form this formula is $\mu\, \mu\, x_1$: inside the inner binder, variable $1$ refers
to the outer binder, not to the inner one.

articles.title: The fixed-point operator of a formula
articles.statement:
Given a Kripke model $M$, an environment $\rho$
(a set of worlds $\rho(n)$ for each variable $n$) and a μ-calculus formula $\varphi$, this is
the monotone map on sets of worlds of $M$ sending $S$ to the set of worlds at which $\varphi$
holds under $\rho[S]$, the extension of $\rho$ under a binder by $S$ (variable $0$ denotes $S$
and variable $n + 1$ denotes $\rho(n)$).

articles.title: Fuelled parsing inverts modal μ-calculus token encoding
articles.statement: Parsing inverts token encoding, with enough fuel.

articles.title: Fuelled parser for modal μ-calculus token lists
The least fixed point is a pre-fixed point
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Kripke model, $\rho$ an
environment and $\varphi$ a μ-calculus formula. Write $\llbracket\psi\rrbracket_\sigma$ for the
set of worlds of $M$ at which $\psi$ holds under the environment $\sigma$, and $\rho[S]$ for the
extension of $\rho$ under a binder by a set of worlds $S$ (variable $0$ denotes $S$ and variable
$n + 1$ denotes $\rho(n)$). For $T = \llbracket\mu\varphi\rrbracket_\rho$, where $\mu\varphi$
binds variable $0$ of $\varphi$, we have $\llbracket\varphi\rrbracket_{\rho[T]} \subseteq T$.

articles.title: Polynomial-size token-list encoding of μ-calculus formulas
articles.statement:
A polynomial-size token-list encoding of μ-calculus formulas over `ℕ`
atoms, used for the complexity statements in `WantedExt`. Each connective
contributes one tag token (`Nat.pair` of a small tag with `0`), and each atom
or variable contributes one token `Nat.pair tag value`, whose binary size is
`O(log value)`. The canonical bitstring encoding of a `List ℕ` delimits each
token, so the bitstring for a formula has length linear in the number of
connectives plus the total binary size of its atoms: `box^d (atom 0)` is
encoded by exactly `d + 1` tokens, unlike its Cantor-paired `muCode`,
whose binary length is exponential in `d`.

articles.title: Meta-level negation is an involution
articles.statement:
Write $
eg\varphi$ for the meta-level negation of
a μ-calculus formula $\varphi$, which swaps each connective with its dual. For every μ-calculus
formula $\varphi$, negating twice gives back $\varphi$: $
eg
eg\varphi = \varphi$.

articles.title: Negation of μ-calculus formulas
articles.statement:
The meta-level negation $
eg\varphi$ of a μ-calculus
formula $\varphi$ swaps each connective with its dual. It is defined by recursion: an atom $p$
becomes the negated atom $\overline{p}$ and $\overline{p}$ becomes $p$, each variable $x_n$
stays $x_n$, $
eg ot = 	op$, $
eg	op =  ot$,
$
eg(\varphi \wedge \psi) = 
eg\varphi \vee 
eg\psi$,
$
eg(\varphi \vee \psi) = 
eg\varphi \wedge 
eg\psi$, $
eg\Box\varphi = \Diamond
eg\varphi$,
$
eg\Diamond\varphi = \Box
eg\varphi$, $
eg\mu\varphi = 
u
eg\varphi$ and
$
eg
u\varphi = \mu
eg\varphi$.

articles.title: Coinduction for the greatest fixed point
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Kripke model, $\rho$ an
environment, $\varphi$ a μ-calculus formula and $P$ a set of worlds of $M$. Write
$\llbracket\psi\rrbracket_\sigma$ for the set of worlds at which $\psi$ holds under the
environment $\sigma$, and $\rho[P]$ for the extension of $\rho$ under a binder by $P$ (variable
$0$ denotes $P$ and variable $n + 1$ denotes $\rho(n)$). If
$P \subseteq \llbracket\varphi\rrbracket_{\rho[P]}$, then
$P \subseteq \llbracket\nu\varphi\rrbracket_\rho$, where $\nu\varphi$ binds variable $0$ of
$\varphi$: every post-fixed point is below the greatest fixed point.

articles.title: The greatest fixed point is a pre-fixed point
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Kripke model, $\rho$ an
environment and $\varphi$ a μ-calculus formula. Write $\llbracket\psi\rrbracket_\sigma$ for the
set of worlds of $M$ at which $\psi$ holds under the environment $\sigma$, and $\rho[S]$ for the
extension of $\rho$ under a binder by a set of worlds $S$ (variable $0$ denotes $S$ and variable
$n + 1$ denotes $\rho(n)$). For $T = \llbracket\nu\varphi\rrbracket_\rho$, where $\nu\varphi$
binds variable $0$ of $\varphi$, we have $\llbracket\varphi\rrbracket_{\rho[T]} \subseteq T$.

articles.title: The formula $\nu X.\, \nu Y.\, X$ is true everywhere
articles.statement:
For every Kripke model $M$ and
every environment $\rho$, the formula $\nu X.\, \nu Y.\, X$ holds at every world of $M$ under
$\rho$. In de Bruijn form this formula is $\nu\, \nu\, x_1$: inside the inner binder, variable
$1$ refers to the outer binder. This is the dual of the fact that $\mu X.\, \mu Y.\, X$ is false
everywhere.

articles.title: The greatest fixed point is a post-fixed point
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Kripke model, $\rho$ an
environment and $\varphi$ a μ-calculus formula. Write $\llbracket\psi\rrbracket_\sigma$ for the
set of worlds of $M$ at which $\psi$ holds under the environment $\sigma$, and $\rho[S]$ for the
extension of $\rho$ under a binder by a set of worlds $S$ (variable $0$ denotes $S$ and variable
$n + 1$ denotes $\rho(n)$). For $T = \llbracket\nu\varphi\rrbracket_\rho$, where $\nu\varphi$
binds variable $0$ of $\varphi$, we have $T \subseteq \llbracket\varphi\rrbracket_{\rho[T]}$.

articles.title: Denotation of a closed μ-calculus formula is environment-independent
articles.statement:
A closed formula does not depend on the environment: environments agreeing below
the depth give the same denotation.

articles.title: Satisfaction is monotone in the environment
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Kripke model and let $\rho$
and $\rho'$ be environments (each assigns a set of worlds of $M$ to every variable $n$) with
$\rho(n) \subseteq \rho'(n)$ for every $n$. Then every μ-calculus formula $\varphi$ holds under
$\rho'$ at every world of $M$ where it holds under $\rho$: enlarging every variable's denotation
can only enlarge a formula's denotation.

articles.title: Monotonicity in the bound variable
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Kripke model, $\rho$ an environment
assigning a set of worlds to each variable index $n \in \mathbb{N}$, and $\varphi$ a μ-calculus
formula. For a set of worlds $S$, write $\rho[0 \mapsto S]$ for the environment sending index $0$
to $S$ and index $n + 1$ to $\rho(n)$. If $S_1 \subseteq S_2$ are sets of worlds, then every world
that satisfies $\varphi$ in $M$ under $\rho[0 \mapsto S_1]$ also satisfies $\varphi$ in $M$ under
$\rho[0 \mapsto S_2]$.

articles.title: The μ formula denotes the least fixed point
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Kripke model, $\rho$ an
environment assigning a set of worlds to each variable index $n \in \mathbb{N}$, and $\varphi$ a
μ-calculus formula. For a set of worlds $S$, write $\rho[0 \mapsto S]$ for the environment sending
index $0$ to $S$ and index $n + 1$ to $\rho(n)$. Then the set of worlds satisfying $\mu\varphi$ in
$M$ under $\rho$ is the least fixed point of the monotone operator on sets of worlds that sends
$S$ to the set of worlds satisfying $\varphi$ in $M$ under $\rho[0 \mapsto S]$.

articles.title: The μ unfolding
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Kripke model, $\rho$ an environment assigning a set of
worlds to each variable index $n \in \mathbb{N}$, and $\varphi$ a μ-calculus formula. Let $A$ be
the set of worlds satisfying $\mu\varphi$ in $M$ under $\rho$. Then $A$ is exactly the set of
worlds satisfying $\varphi$ in $M$ under the environment that sends index $0$ to $A$ and index
$n + 1$ to $\rho(n)$.

articles.title: Duality
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Kripke model, $\rho$ an environment assigning a set of worlds to
each variable index $n \in \mathbb{N}$, and $\varphi$ a μ-calculus formula. Let $\neg\varphi$ be
the dual formula of $\varphi$, obtained by swapping atoms with negated atoms, $\bot$ with $\top$,
$\wedge$ with $\vee$, $\Box$ with $\Diamond$ and $\mu$ with $\nu$, and keeping variables. Write
$\overline{\rho}$ for the environment sending each index $n$ to the complement of $\rho(n)$. Then
for every world $w$, $w$ satisfies $\neg\varphi$ in $M$ under $\overline{\rho}$ if and only if $w$
does not satisfy $\varphi$ in $M$ under $\rho$.

articles.title: The ν formula denotes the greatest fixed point
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Kripke model, $\rho$ an
environment assigning a set of worlds to each variable index $n \in \mathbb{N}$, and $\varphi$ a
μ-calculus formula. For a set of worlds $S$, write $\rho[0 \mapsto S]$ for the environment sending
index $0$ to $S$ and index $n + 1$ to $\rho(n)$. Then the set of worlds satisfying $\nu\varphi$ in
$M$ under $\rho$ is the greatest fixed point of the monotone operator on sets of worlds that sends
$S$ to the set of worlds satisfying $\varphi$ in $M$ under $\rho[0 \mapsto S]$.

articles.title: The ν unfolding
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Kripke model, $\rho$ an environment assigning a set of
worlds to each variable index $n \in \mathbb{N}$, and $\varphi$ a μ-calculus formula. Let $A$ be
the set of worlds satisfying $\nu\varphi$ in $M$ under $\rho$. Then $A$ is exactly the set of
worlds satisfying $\varphi$ in $M$ under the environment that sends index $0$ to $A$ and index
$n + 1$ to $\rho(n)$.

articles.title: Satisfaction in the modal μ-calculus
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Kripke model with accessibility
relation $R$ and valuation $V$, and let $\rho$ be an environment assigning a set of worlds to
each variable index $n \in \mathbb{N}$. For a set of worlds $S$, write $\rho[0 \mapsto S]$ for the
environment sending index $0$ to $S$ and index $n + 1$ to $\rho(n)$. The set $[\![\varphi]\!]_\rho$
of worlds satisfying a formula $\varphi$ in $M$ under $\rho$ is defined by recursion on
$\varphi$: an atom $a$ holds at $w$ when $V$ makes $a$ true at $w$, and the negated atom of $a$
when $V$ does not; the variable with index $n$ denotes $\rho(n)$; $\bot$ holds nowhere and $\top$
everywhere; conjunction and disjunction denote intersection and union; $\Box\varphi$ holds at $w$
when $\varphi$ holds at every $v$ with $w \mathrel{R} v$, and $\Diamond\varphi$ when $\varphi$
holds at some such $v$; $\mu\varphi$ holds at $w$ when $w \in S$ for every set of worlds $S$ with
$[\![\varphi]\!]_{\rho[0 \mapsto S]} \subseteq S$; and $\nu\varphi$ holds at $w$ when $w \in S$
for some set of worlds $S$ with $S \subseteq [\![\varphi]\!]_{\rho[0 \mapsto S]}$.

So $\mu\varphi$ is the least pre-fixed point of $S \mapsto [\![\varphi]\!]_{\rho[0 \mapsto S]}$,
stated directly as an infimum over pre-fixed points, and $\nu\varphi$ is the greatest
post-fixed point, stated as a supremum over post-fixed points.

articles.title: The canonical move follows the bespoke strategy at Verifier positions with a move
articles.statement:
Let
$M$ be a Kripke model, $\mathit{env}$ an environment and $\sigma$ a Verifier strategy for the
model-checking game on $M$. Write $\langle \psi, v \rangle$ for the game position with the
embedding of a fixpoint-free formula $\psi$, the world $v$ and the empty binder stack. Let
$\varphi$ be a fixpoint-free formula and $w$ a world such that Verifier owns
$\langle \varphi, w \rangle$ and $\langle \varphi, w \rangle$ has a move to some
$\langle \varphi'', w'' \rangle$. Then there are a fixpoint-free formula $\varphi'$ and a world
$w'$ such that the canonical next move induced by $\sigma$ (in environment $\mathit{env}$) sends
the fragment position $(\varphi, w)$ to the fragment position $(\varphi', w')$, and $\sigma$
chooses $\langle \varphi', w' \rangle$ at $\langle \varphi, w \rangle$.

articles.title: Verifier's positional strategies make a game move at Verifier positions that have one
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Kripke model, $\mathit{env}$ an environment, and $\sigma$ any positional strategy of
the even player (Verifier) in the fragment game of $M$ and $\mathit{env}$. Write
$\langle \psi, v \rangle$ for the game position with the embedding of a fixpoint-free formula
$\psi$, the world $v$ and the empty binder stack. Let $\varphi$ be a fixpoint-free formula and
$w$ a world such that the even player owns the fragment position $(\varphi, w)$ and, in the
model-checking game on $M$, $\langle \varphi, w \rangle$ has a move to some
$\langle \varphi'', w'' \rangle$. Then $\sigma$ sends $(\varphi, w)$ to a fragment position
$(\varphi', w')$ such that $\langle \varphi, w \rangle$ has a move to
$\langle \varphi', w' \rangle$; in particular $\sigma$ does not move to the absorbing state
$\mathrm{win}$ or $\mathrm{lose}$.

articles.title: Canonical next move induced by a bespoke strategy
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Kripke model,
$\mathit{env}$ an environment and $\sigma$ a Verifier strategy for the model-checking game on
$M$. Write $\langle \psi, v \rangle$ for the game position with the embedding of a
fixpoint-free formula $\psi$, the world $v$ and the empty binder stack. The canonical next move
is the map on positions of the fragment arena defined as follows. The absorbing states
$\mathrm{win}$ and $\mathrm{lose}$ are sent to themselves. A fragment position $(\varphi, w)$
such that $\langle \varphi, w \rangle$ has a move to some $\langle \varphi', w' \rangle$ is
sent, if Verifier owns $\langle \varphi, w \rangle$, to the projection into the fragment arena
of the position that $\sigma$ chooses there (an embedded position $\langle \varphi', w' \rangle$
projects to $(\varphi', w')$, every other game position to $\mathrm{lose}$), and otherwise to a
fragment position $(\varphi', w')$ chosen, by the axiom of choice, among those with a move from
$\langle \varphi, w \rangle$ to $\langle \varphi', w' \rangle$. A fragment position
$(\varphi, w)$ with no such move is sent to $\mathrm{win}$ if $\langle \varphi, w \rangle$
satisfies the terminal winning condition for Verifier in environment $\mathit{env}$, and to
$\mathrm{lose}$ otherwise.

articles.title: Segments of canonical plays through fragment positions are bespoke plays
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a
Kripke model, $\mathit{env}$ an environment and $\sigma$ a Verifier strategy for the
model-checking game on $M$. Write $\langle \psi, v \rangle$ for the game position with the
embedding of a fixpoint-free formula $\psi$, the world $v$ and the empty binder stack. Let $\pi$
be a play of the fragment game of $M$ and $\mathit{env}$ that conforms to the canonical
positional strategy induced by $\sigma$, and let $s, k \in \mathbb{N}$. Suppose every $\pi_i$
with $s \le i \le s + k$ is a fragment position $(\varphi_i, w_i)$, not $\mathrm{win}$ or
$\mathrm{lose}$. Then the list
$\langle \varphi_s, w_s \rangle, \langle \varphi_{s+1}, w_{s+1} \rangle, \dots,
\langle \varphi_{s+k}, w_{s+k} \rangle$ is a finite play from $\langle \varphi_s, w_s \rangle$
consistent with $\sigma$: each position has a game move to the next, and at Verifier-owned
positions the next position is the one $\sigma$ chooses.

articles.title: Regression cycle, first step
articles.statement:
Let $\Phi = \mu X.\, \nu Y.\, X$ be the regression formula,
$\ast$ the unique world, and write game positions as (formula, world, stack of enclosing
binders, innermost first). The step map of the regression play sends the first cycle position
$(\Phi, \ast, [\,])$ to the second cycle position $(\nu Y.\, X, \ast, [\Phi])$.

articles.title: Regression cycle, second step
articles.statement:
Let $\Phi = \mu X.\, \nu Y.\, X$ be the regression formula,
$\ast$ the unique world, and write game positions as (formula, world, stack of enclosing
binders, innermost first). The step map of the regression play sends the second cycle position
$(\nu Y.\, X, \ast, [\Phi])$ to the third cycle position $(X, \ast, [\nu Y.\, X, \Phi])$, where
$X$ is the variable bound by the outer $\mu$.

articles.title: Regression cycle, third step
articles.statement:
Let $\Phi = \mu X.\, \nu Y.\, X$ be the regression formula,
$\ast$ the unique world, and write game positions as (formula, world, stack of enclosing
binders, innermost first). The step map of the regression play sends the third cycle position
$(X, \ast, [\nu Y.\, X, \Phi])$, where $X$ is the variable bound by the outer $\mu$, back to
the first cycle position $(\Phi, \ast, [\,])$.

articles.title: Step map of the regression play
articles.statement:
Let $\Phi = \mu X.\, \nu Y.\, X$ be the regression
formula over the one-element type of atoms, and write game positions over the one-element type
of worlds as (formula, world, stack of enclosing binders, innermost first). For every world $w$,
the step map sends $(\Phi, w, [\,])$ to $(\nu Y.\, X, w, [\Phi])$, sends
$(\nu Y.\, X, w, [\Phi])$ to $(X, w, [\nu Y.\, X, \Phi])$, and sends
$(X, w, [\nu Y.\, X, \Phi])$ to $(\Phi, w, [\,])$, where $X$ is the variable bound by the
outer $\mu$; every other game position is sent to itself.

articles.title: The regression play stays on the cycle
articles.statement:
For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the position at
step $n$ of the regression play is the first, the second or the third cycle position.

articles.title: The regression play is a play
articles.statement:
For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, in the model-checking game
on the one-world regression model there is a move from the position at step $n$ of the
regression play to the position at step $n + 1$.

articles.title: The regression play returns to its start every three steps
articles.statement:
Number the positions of
the regression play of $\mu X.\,\nu Y.\,X$ from $0$. For every natural number $k$, its
position number $3k$ is its starting position: the formula $\mu X.\,\nu Y.\,X$ at the unique
world, with the empty binder stack.

articles.title: The regression play has period three
articles.statement:
Number the positions of the regression play
from $0$. For every natural number $n$, its position number $n + 3$ equals its position
number $n$.

articles.title: The regression play
articles.statement:
Write $\ast$ for the unique world, and consider the game positions
(formula, world, binder stack listed innermost first)
$P_0 = (\mu X.\,\nu Y.\,X,\ \ast,\ [\,])$, $P_1 = (\nu Y.\,X,\ \ast,\ [\mu X.\,\nu Y.\,X])$ and
$P_2 = (X,\ \ast,\ [\nu Y.\,X,\ \mu X.\,\nu Y.\,X])$. Let $s$ be the step map sending $P_0$ to
$P_1$, $P_1$ to $P_2$ and $P_2$ to $P_0$, and fixing every other position. The regression play is
the sequence of positions $p_0 = P_0$, $p_{n+1} = s(p_n)$, which cycles through $P_0, P_1, P_2$.

These are the successive positions of the model-checking game for $\mu X.\,\nu Y.\,X$ on the
one-world model.

articles.title: Starting position of the regression play
articles.statement:
The game position consisting of the formula
$\mu X.\,\nu Y.\,X$, the unique world of the one-world model, and the empty binder stack.

articles.title: Second position of the regression play
articles.statement:
The game position consisting of the formula
$\nu Y.\,X$, the unique world of the one-world model, and the binder stack
$[\mu X.\,\nu Y.\,X]$. Here $X$ is the de Bruijn variable $1$, which refers to the binder
$\mu X$ on the stack.

articles.title: Third position of the regression play
articles.statement:
The game position consisting of the variable $X$,
the unique world of the one-world model, and the binder stack $[\nu Y.\,X,\ \mu X.\,\nu Y.\,X]$,
listed innermost first. Here $X$ is the de Bruijn variable $1$, which refers to the outer binder
$\mu X$.

articles.title: Priority of the outer binder in the regression play
articles.statement:
The starting position of the
regression play, consisting of the formula $\mu X.\,\nu Y.\,X$, the unique world and the empty
binder stack, has priority $1$: a $\mu$-binder position with $k$ binders on the stack has
priority $2k + 1$, and here $k = 0$.

Under fixed priorities ($\mu \mapsto 1$, $\nu \mapsto 2$) the greatest priority recurring on this
play would be $2$ (even, Verifier wins); with priorities increasing with nesting depth (the inner
$\nu$ here has priority $4$) and the least-priority rule, the least binder priority recurring on
this play is $1$ (odd, Refuter wins).

articles.title: Priority of the inner binder in the regression play
articles.statement:
The second position of the
regression play, consisting of the formula $\nu Y.\,X$, the unique world and the binder stack
$[\mu X.\,\nu Y.\,X]$, has priority $4$: a $\nu$-binder position with $k$ binders on the stack
has priority $2k + 2$, and here $k = 1$.

articles.title: Formulas closed at depth $d$
articles.statement:
Closedness of a μ-calculus formula $\varphi$ (with de Bruijn
variables) at a depth $d \in \mathbb{N}$ is defined by recursion on $\varphi$: atoms, negated
atoms, $\bot$ and $\top$ are closed at every depth; the variable with index $n$ is closed at
depth $d$ exactly when $n < d$; $\varphi \wedge \psi$ and $\varphi \vee \psi$ are closed at
depth $d$ when both $\varphi$ and $\psi$ are; $\Box\varphi$ and $\Diamond\varphi$ are closed at
depth $d$ when $\varphi$ is; and $\mu\varphi$ and $\nu\varphi$ are closed at depth $d$ when
$\varphi$ is closed at depth $d + 1$. Thus every free variable of $\varphi$ refers to one of $d$
enclosing binders.

## Sources

- C. Stirling, *Modal and Temporal Properties of Processes*, Springer 2001, Chapter 6 (de Bruijn variables).

articles.title: Closed formulas
articles.statement:
A μ-calculus formula $\varphi$ is closed when it is closed at depth $0$,
that is, when it has no free variables.

articles.title: A least fixpoint over a vacuous greatest fixpoint
articles.statement:
The μ-calculus formula
$\mu X.\, \nu Y.\, X$ over a one-element type of atoms: a least fixpoint whose body is a greatest
fixpoint whose body is the variable $X$ bound by the outer least fixpoint, so the variable $Y$
bound by the inner greatest fixpoint never occurs.

Its denotation is empty: the outer functional is the identity, and the least fixed point of the
identity on predicates is the empty predicate.

articles.title: The one-world reflexive Kripke model
articles.statement:
The Kripke model with a single world, which is
related to itself, and a single atom, which is false at that world.

articles.title: Verifier loses the infinite play of $\mu X.\, \nu Y.\, X$
articles.statement:
Consider the infinite
sequence of positions of the model-checking game for $\mu X.\, \nu Y.\, X$ (with one-element
types of worlds and atoms) that starts at this formula with empty binder stack and repeats three
steps: unfold $\mu X$, unfold $\nu Y$, and follow the variable $X$ back to the formula with empty
stack. This play does not satisfy the parity condition: it is not the case that the least binder
priority occurring infinitely often is even.

articles.title: $\mu X.\, \nu Y.\, X$ is false in the one-world model
articles.statement:
In the Kripke model with a single
world, which is related to itself, and a single atom, which is false there, under the environment
that assigns the empty set to every variable, the formula $\mu X.\, \nu Y.\, X$ is not satisfied
at the unique world.

This agrees with the model-checking game, where Verifier loses the play of this formula.

articles.title: Moves from a diamond position
articles.statement:
In the model-checking game on a Kripke model $M$, every
move from the position with formula $\Diamond\varphi$, world $w$ and binder stack $s$ goes to the
position with formula $\varphi$, world $v$ and the same stack $s$, for some world $v$ accessible
from $w$ in $M$.

articles.title: Fixpoint-free formulas
articles.statement:
The fixpoint-free formulas over a type of atoms are built from
atoms $p$, negated atoms $\neg p$, $\bot$ and $\top$ by conjunction $\varphi \land \psi$,
disjunction $\varphi \lor \psi$, necessity $\Box\varphi$ and possibility $\Diamond\varphi$.

These are the formulas of basic modal logic in negation normal form: the μ-calculus formulas with
no fixpoint operators and no variables.

articles.title: Moves of the totalized fragment game, by cases
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Kripke model and $e$ an
environment, and read each fixpoint-free formula $\varphi$ as a μ-calculus formula. Every move
from $a$ to $b$ in the totalized fragment game of $M$ and $e$ is of one of five kinds: $a$ and $b$
are embedded positions $(\varphi, w)$ and $(\varphi', w')$ and the model-checking game of $M$ has a
move from $(\varphi, w)$ to $(\varphi', w')$ with empty binder stacks; or $a = (\varphi, w)$, $b$ is
the winning state, and the game position $(\varphi, w)$ with empty stack has no moves and is won by
Verifier in environment $e$; or $a = (\varphi, w)$, $b$ is the losing state, and that game position
has no moves and is not won by Verifier; or $a$ and $b$ are both the winning state; or $a$ and $b$
are both the losing state.

articles.title: Moves of the totalized fragment game
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Kripke model and $e$ an environment,
and read each fixpoint-free formula $\varphi$ as a μ-calculus formula. The totalized fragment game
of $M$ and $e$ has these moves: from an embedded position $(\varphi, w)$ to $(\varphi', w')$
whenever the model-checking game of $M$ has a move from $(\varphi, w)$ to $(\varphi', w')$ with
empty binder stacks; from $(\varphi, w)$ to the winning state when the game position
$(\varphi, w)$ with empty stack has no moves and is won by Verifier in environment $e$; from
$(\varphi, w)$ to the losing state when that game position has no moves and is not won by
Verifier; and from each of the winning and losing states to itself.

articles.title: Projection of an embedded position
articles.statement:
For every fixpoint-free formula $\varphi$ and world
$w$, projecting the game position with formula $\varphi$ (read as a μ-calculus formula), world $w$
and empty binder stack onto the fragment arena gives the embedded position $(\varphi, w)$.

articles.title: Projection of game positions onto the fragment arena
articles.statement:
A game position with empty binder
stack whose formula is the μ-calculus reading of a fixpoint-free formula $\varphi$, at world $w$,
is sent to the embedded position $(\varphi, w)$. Every other game position (one whose formula
contains a fixpoint operator or a variable, or one with a nonempty stack) is sent to the losing
state.

The losing state is a default that is never reached on plays that stay in the arena, since every
move from an embedded position lands on an embedded position.

## Sources

- C. Stirling, *Modal and Temporal Properties of Processes*, Springer 2001, Chapter 6.

articles.title: Owner of an embedded position in the totalized fragment game
articles.statement:
For every fixpoint-free
formula $\varphi$ and world $w$, the even player owns the embedded position $(\varphi, w)$ of the
totalized fragment game if and only if Verifier owns the model-checking game position
$(\varphi, w, [])$, with $\varphi$ embedded as a μ-calculus formula and the empty fixpoint stack.

articles.title: Owners in the totalized fragment game
articles.statement:
In the totalized fragment game, an embedded
position $(\varphi, w)$ of a fixpoint-free formula $\varphi$ at a world $w$ is owned by the even
player if Verifier owns the model-checking game position $(\varphi, w, [])$ (with $\varphi$
embedded as a μ-calculus formula and the empty fixpoint stack), and by the odd player otherwise,
that is, when Refuter owns it. The absorbing winning and losing states are both owned by the
even player.

Verifier plays the even player; the moves at the absorbing states are forced, so their owner
does not matter.

articles.title: Plays of the totalized fragment game stay at the losing state
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Kripke model
and $\mathit{env}$ an environment assigning a set of worlds to each free-variable index. If
$\pi$ is a play of the totalized fragment game of $M$ and $\mathit{env}$ and $\pi_k$ is the
absorbing losing state, then $\pi_n$ is the losing state for every $n \ge k$.

articles.title: Plays of the totalized fragment game stay at the winning state
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Kripke model
and $\mathit{env}$ an environment assigning a set of worlds to each free-variable index. If
$\pi$ is a play of the totalized fragment game of $M$ and $\mathit{env}$ and $\pi_k$ is the
absorbing winning state, then $\pi_n$ is the winning state for every $n \ge k$.

articles.title: Terminal losing positions are not won by the even player
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Kripke model,
$\mathit{env}$ an environment assigning a set of worlds to each free-variable index, $\varphi$ a
fixpoint-free formula and $w$ a world. If the model-checking game position $(\varphi, w, [])$,
with $\varphi$ embedded as a μ-calculus formula and the empty fixpoint stack, has no moves in $M$
and is not a terminal win for Verifier in $M$ under $\mathit{env}$, then the embedded position
$(\varphi, w)$ of the totalized fragment game of $M$ and $\mathit{env}$ is not in the winning
region of the even player.

The play that moves from $(\varphi, w)$ to the losing state and stays there conforms to every
strategy of the even player and is won by the odd player.

articles.title: Positions of the totalized fragment game
articles.statement:
A position of the totalized fragment game, over
a type of atoms and a type of worlds, is either an embedded position $(\varphi, w)$ of a
fixpoint-free formula $\varphi$ and a world $w$, standing for the model-checking game position
$(\varphi, w, [])$ with $\varphi$ embedded as a μ-calculus formula and the empty fixpoint stack,
or one of two absorbing states: the winning state, where Verifier has won, and the losing state,
where Refuter has won.

Since the arena contains no fixpoint positions and every move between embedded positions
strictly decreases the formula, priority $0$ on embedded positions is sound. An embedded
position with no moves leads to the winning state if it is a terminal win for Verifier and to
the losing state otherwise, and both absorbing states loop to themselves, so the game has no
dead ends and is a parity game.

articles.title: Priorities in the totalized fragment game
articles.statement:
In the totalized fragment game, every embedded
position $(\varphi, w)$ of a fixpoint-free formula $\varphi$ at a world $w$ has priority $0$, the
absorbing winning state has priority $0$, and the absorbing losing state has priority $1$.

So an infinite play that eventually stays at the winning state is won by the even player, and
one that eventually stays at the losing state by the odd player. Priority $0$ on embedded
positions is sound because the arena contains no fixpoint positions and every move between
embedded positions strictly decreases the formula, so no infinite play visits only embedded
positions.

articles.title: Splitting off the head of a segment
articles.statement:
Let $p_0$ be a model-checking game position and $\pi$
an infinite sequence of positions of the totalized fragment game. For each $i$, let $\hat\pi_i$ be
$p_0$ if $\pi_i$ is an absorbing state; if $\pi_i$ is the embedded position $(\varphi, w)$ of a
fixpoint-free formula $\varphi$ and a world $w$, let $\hat\pi_i$ be the game position
$(\varphi, w, [])$, with $\varphi$ embedded as a μ-calculus formula and the empty fixpoint stack.
For all natural numbers $s$ and $k$, the segment $[\hat\pi_s, \dots, \hat\pi_{s+k+1}]$ of $\pi$ is
the list with head $\hat\pi_s$ followed by the segment $[\hat\pi_{s+1}, \dots, \hat\pi_{s+k+1}]$.

articles.title: Segments are nonempty
articles.statement:
Let $p_0$ be a model-checking game position and $\pi$ an infinite
sequence of positions of the totalized fragment game. For all natural numbers $s$ and $k$, the
segment of $\pi$ from index $s$ to index $s + k$, read as a list of model-checking game positions
with $p_0$ standing for the absorbing states, is not the empty list.

articles.title: Last position of a segment
articles.statement:
Let $p_0$ be a model-checking game position and $\pi$ an
infinite sequence of positions of the totalized fragment game. For each $i$, let $\hat\pi_i$ be
$p_0$ if $\pi_i$ is an absorbing state; if $\pi_i$ is the embedded position $(\varphi, w)$ of a
fixpoint-free formula $\varphi$ and a world $w$, let $\hat\pi_i$ be the game position
$(\varphi, w, [])$, with $\varphi$ embedded as a μ-calculus formula and the empty fixpoint stack.
For all natural numbers $s$ and $k$, the segment $[\hat\pi_s, \dots, \hat\pi_{s+k}]$ has a last
position, and it is $\hat\pi_{s+k}$.

articles.title: Segment of a fragment play as game positions
articles.statement:
Let $p_0$ be a game position and let
$\pi = \pi_0 \pi_1 \pi_2 \dots$ be an infinite sequence of positions of the totalized fragment
game. For natural numbers $s$ and $k$, the segment of $\pi$ from $s$ of length $k + 1$ is the
list of game positions obtained from $\pi_s, \pi_{s+1}, \dots, \pi_{s+k}$, in this order, by
sending each embedded position $(\varphi, w)$ to the game position with formula $\varphi$, world
$w$ and empty binder stack, and each of the absorbing winning and losing states to $p_0$.

articles.title: Positional strategy induced by a bespoke strategy
articles.statement: The canonical positional strategy induced by a bespoke strategy.

articles.title: Game position of a fragment position
articles.statement:
Given a default game position $p_0$, an embedded
fragment position $(\varphi, w)$ is sent to the game position with formula $\varphi$, world $w$
and empty binder stack, and the absorbing winning and losing states are both sent to $p_0$.

The default is never used on plays that stay among embedded positions.

articles.title: Winning Verifier strategies transfer to the fragment game
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Kripke model,
$\rho$ an environment, $\sigma$ a Verifier strategy of the model-checking game on $M$,
$\varphi$ a fixpoint-free formula and $w$ a world. If $\sigma$ wins in environment $\rho$ from
the game position with formula $\varphi$, world $w$ and empty binder stack, then the positional
strategy of the even player induced by $\sigma$ wins from the embedded position $(\varphi, w)$
in the fragment game of $M$ and $\rho$.

Every play conforming to the induced strategy reaches the absorbing winning state: it cannot
reach the losing state, by the finite-play clause for $\sigma$ applied to the segment before the
first losing state, and it cannot stay among embedded positions forever, since fragment moves
strictly decrease the formula.

articles.title: The fragment game's winning region is contained in Wins
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Kripke model,
$\rho$ an environment, $\varphi$ a fixpoint-free formula and $w$ a world. If the embedded
position $(\varphi, w)$ lies in the winning region of the even player in the fragment game of
$M$ and $\rho$, then the backward-induction winning condition $\mathrm{Wins}_M(\varphi, w)$
holds.

The proof is by induction on $\varphi$, using that the winning region is closed under the
opponent's moves and under the moves of a winning strategy, so no strategy composition is
needed.

articles.title: Fragment parity game
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Kripke model and $\rho$ an environment, and write
$(\varphi, w, [])$ for the game position with formula $\varphi$, world $w$ and empty binder
stack. The fragment game of $M$ and $\rho$ is the parity game on the totalized fragment
positions defined as follows. An embedded position $(\varphi, w)$ moves to $(\varphi', w')$
when $(\varphi, w, [])$ has a move to $(\varphi', w', [])$ in the model-checking game on $M$;
if $(\varphi, w, [])$ has no moves, $(\varphi, w)$ moves to the winning state when
$(\varphi, w, [])$ is a terminal win in $\rho$ and to the losing state otherwise; the winning
and losing states move only to themselves. The even player owns both absorbing states and the
embedded positions $(\varphi, w)$ such that Verifier owns $(\varphi, w, [])$; the odd player
owns the other embedded positions. Embedded positions and the winning state have priority $0$;
the losing state has priority $1$.

articles.title: Wins is the winning region of the fragment game
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Kripke model, $\rho$ an
environment, $\varphi$ a fixpoint-free formula and $w$ a world. Then the backward-induction
winning condition $\mathrm{Wins}_M(\varphi, w)$ holds if and only if the embedded position
$(\varphi, w)$ lies in the winning region of the even player in the fragment game of $M$ and
$\rho$.

articles.title: Position of the μ-calculus model-checking game
articles.statement:
A position of the μ-calculus model-checking game: the formula, the world, and
the stack of enclosing fixpoint binders, innermost first.

articles.title: The losing state is absorbing
articles.statement:
In the fragment game of a Kripke model $M$ and an
environment $\rho$, every move from the losing state goes to the losing state.

articles.title: The lose play stays at the losing state
articles.statement:
For every fixpoint-free formula $\varphi$,
world $w$ and natural number $n$, the lose play from $(\varphi, w)$ is at the losing state at
time $n + 1$.

articles.title: The lose play starts at its fragment position
articles.statement:
For a fixpoint-free formula $\varphi$
and a world $w$, the lose play from $(\varphi, w)$ is at the fragment-arena position
$(\varphi, w)$ at time $0$.

articles.title: The lose play
articles.statement:
For a fixpoint-free formula $\varphi$ and a world $w$, the lose play is the
infinite sequence of positions of the fragment arena that is at the position $(\varphi, w)$ at
time $0$ and at the absorbing losing state at every later time. It is used for terminal losing
positions $(\varphi, w)$.

articles.title: Closedness is monotone in the depth
articles.statement:
Let $\varphi$ be a μ-calculus formula and let
$d \le d'$ be natural numbers. If $\varphi$ is closed at depth $d$ (every free variable of
$\varphi$ is less than $d$), then $\varphi$ is closed at depth $d'$: more enclosing binders can
only bind more variables.

articles.title: Fragment moves decrease the formula size
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Kripke model, $\varphi$ a
fixpoint-free formula and $w$ a world. Every move of the model-checking game in $M$ from the
position $(\varphi, w, [\,])$, with $\varphi$ embedded in the μ-calculus and the empty stack, leads
to a position $(\varphi', w', [\,])$ for some fixpoint-free formula $\varphi'$ and world $w'$,
and the size of $\varphi'$ is strictly smaller than the size of $\varphi$ (sizes of the embedded
μ-calculus formulas).

articles.title: Moves of the μ-calculus model-checking game
articles.statement:
Fix a Kripke model $M$ with accessibility
relation $R$. A game position $(\varphi, w, s)$ consists of a μ-calculus formula $\varphi$ (with
de Bruijn variables), a world $w$ and a stack $s$ of fixpoint binders, innermost first. The
moves are exactly the following. From $(\varphi \wedge \psi, w, s)$ and from
$(\varphi \vee \psi, w, s)$ to $(\varphi, w, s)$ and to $(\psi, w, s)$. From
$(\Box \varphi, w, s)$ and from $(\Diamond \varphi, w, s)$ to $(\varphi, v, s)$ for every world
$v$ with $w R v$. From $(\mu \varphi, w, s)$ to $(\varphi, w, s')$, where $s'$ is $s$ with
$\mu \varphi$ pushed on top, and likewise from $(\nu \varphi, w, s)$ to $(\varphi, w, s'')$,
where $s''$ is $s$ with $\nu \varphi$ pushed on top. From $(x_n, w, s)$, where $x_n$ is the
variable with de Bruijn index $n$ and $n$ is less than the length of $s$, to $(s_n, w, t)$,
where $s_n$ is the entry of $s$ at index $n$ (counting from $0$) and $t$ is $s$ with its first
$n + 1$ entries removed.

## Sources

- C. Stirling, *Modal and Temporal Properties of Processes*, Springer 2001, Chapter 6.

articles.title: Finite plays are nonempty
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Kripke model, $\sigma$ a Verifier strategy and
$p$ a game position. Every finite play from $p$ consistent with $\sigma$ is a nonempty list of
positions.

articles.title: No infinite play from a fragment position
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Kripke model, $\varphi$ a
fixpoint-free formula and $w$ a world. There is no sequence of game positions
$p_0, p_1, p_2, \dots$ with $p_0 = (\varphi, w, [\,])$ (the embedded formula with the empty
stack) such that each step from $p_n$ to $p_{n+1}$ is a move of the model-checking game in $M$.
The reason is that every move strictly decreases the formula size.

articles.title: Positions with no moves
articles.statement:
In a Kripke model $M$, a game position $p$ has no moves when
there is no position $q$ such that going from $p$ to $q$ is a move of the model-checking game
in $M$.

articles.title: Inversion for disjunction moves
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Kripke model, $\varphi$ and $\psi$
μ-calculus formulas, $w$ a world and $s$ a stack of fixpoint binders. If going from the game
position $(\varphi \vee \psi, w, s)$ to a position $q$ is a move of the model-checking game in
$M$, then $q$ is $(\varphi, w, s)$ or $(\psi, w, s)$: the world and the stack are unchanged.

articles.title: Owner of a game position
articles.statement:
The owner of a game position $(\varphi, w, s)$ is Verifier when
$\varphi$ is a disjunction, a diamond formula or a greatest fixed point, and Refuter for every
other formula.

## Sources

- C. Stirling, *Modal and Temporal Properties of Processes*, Springer 2001, Chapter 6.

articles.title: Parity winning condition
articles.statement:
For an infinite sequence of game positions $p_0, p_1, \dots$,
Verifier wins by the parity condition when there is an even priority $e$ such that infinitely
many positions $p_n$ have priority $e$, and every priority $e' < e$ is the priority of only
finitely many positions $p_n$. Equivalently, some priority occurs infinitely often and the least
such priority is even; in particular, if no priority occurs infinitely often, Verifier does not
win. Only fixpoint-binder positions carry a priority, so the other positions do not affect the
outcome.

The least-priority convention is what makes outer binders dominate: an outer binder has a smaller
priority than any binder nested inside it.

## Sources

- E. A. Emerson and C. S. Jutla, "Tree automata, μ-calculus and determinacy", *Proceedings of FOCS 1991*, 368-377.

articles.title: Finite plays consistent with a strategy
articles.statement:
Fix a Kripke model $M$ and a Verifier strategy
$\sigma$. The finite plays from a position $p$ that follow $\sigma$ are the lists of positions
defined inductively: the one-element list $[p]$ is such a play; and if the game has a move from
$p$ to $q$, where $q$ is the position chosen by $\sigma$ at $p$ whenever Verifier owns $p$, then
$p$ followed by any such play from $q$ is such a play from $p$.

A play need not end at a position with no moves: every finite prefix counts.

articles.title: Prepending to a nonempty play keeps the last position
articles.statement:
For a game position $p$ and a
nonempty list $ps$ of game positions, the list obtained by prepending $p$ to $ps$ has the same
last position as $ps$.

articles.title: Last position of a play
articles.statement:
The last position of a finite list of game positions is its
final entry when the list is nonempty; the empty list has no last position.

articles.title: Player of the μ-calculus model-checking game
articles.statement: The player to move: `true` is Verifier, `false` is Refuter.

articles.title: Fragment moves between embedded positions are game moves
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Kripke model,
$\mathrm{env}$ an environment, $\varphi, \varphi'$ fixpoint-free formulas and $w, w'$ worlds. If
the totalized fragment game has a move from the embedded position $(\varphi, w)$ to the embedded
position $(\varphi', w')$, then the model-checking game has a move from $(\varphi, w, [])$ to
$(\varphi', w', [])$, where the fixpoint-free formulas are viewed as μ-calculus formulas and
$[]$ is the empty binder stack.

articles.title: Moves to the losing state come from terminal losing positions
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Kripke model,
$\mathrm{env}$ an environment, $\varphi$ a fixpoint-free formula and $w$ a world. If the
totalized fragment game has a move from the embedded position $(\varphi, w)$ to the absorbing
losing state, then the game position $(\varphi, w, [])$, with $\varphi$ viewed as a μ-calculus
formula and an empty binder stack, has no moves, and Verifier does not win there as a terminal
position in the environment $\mathrm{env}$.

articles.title: Moves to the winning state come from terminal winning positions
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Kripke
model, $\mathrm{env}$ an environment, $\varphi$ a fixpoint-free formula and $w$ a world. If the
totalized fragment game has a move from the embedded position $(\varphi, w)$ to the absorbing
winning state, then the game position $(\varphi, w, [])$, with $\varphi$ viewed as a μ-calculus
formula and an empty binder stack, has no moves, and Verifier wins there as a terminal position
in the environment $\mathrm{env}$.

articles.title: Priority of a game position
articles.statement:
Only fixpoint-binder positions carry a priority. For a
formula $\varphi$, a world $w$ and a binder stack $s$ of length $k$, the position
$(\mu X.\,\varphi, w, s)$, whose formula is the least fixpoint with body $\varphi$, has priority
$2k+1$, the position $(\nu X.\,\varphi, w, s)$, whose formula is the greatest fixpoint with body
$\varphi$, has priority $2k+2$, and every other position has no priority. Priorities strictly
increase with nesting depth, so the outermost binder regenerated infinitely often has the least
priority.

This is the nesting-depth refinement of the alternation-depth priority assignment: same-type
nesting counts toward the depth, which only refines the order (outer still strictly below inner)
and keeps parity tied to the binder kind. Fixed priorities ($\mu \mapsto 1$, $\nu \mapsto 2$)
under the greatest-recurring-priority rule would let an inner vacuous $\nu$ dominate an outer
$\mu$: in $\mu X.\,\nu Y.\,X$, whose denotation is empty, Verifier would win the only play.

## Sources

- E. A. Emerson and C. S. Jutla, "Tree automata, μ-calculus and determinacy", *Proceedings of FOCS 1991*, 368-377; C. Stirling, *Modal and Temporal Properties of Processes*, Springer 2001, Chapter 6; J. A. Bradfield, "The modal μ-calculus alternation hierarchy is strict", *Theoretical Computer Science* 195 (1998), 133-153 (alternation depth).

articles.title: Closed formulas are environment-independent
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Kripke model and $\varphi$ a
closed μ-calculus formula, that is, one with no free variables. For any two environments
$\mathrm{env}$ and $\mathrm{env}'$, each assigning a set of worlds to every variable index, and
every world $w$, $\varphi$ is satisfied at $w$ in $M$ under $\mathrm{env}$ if and only if it is
satisfied at $w$ in $M$ under $\mathrm{env}'$.

articles.title: Satisfaction depends only on the environment below the closure depth
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a
Kripke model, $\varphi$ a μ-calculus formula and $d$ a natural number such that $\varphi$ is
closed at depth $d$: every occurrence of a variable with de Bruijn index $n$ lying under $k$
fixpoint binders of $\varphi$ satisfies $n < d + k$. If two environments $\mathit{env}$ and
$\mathit{env}'$, each assigning a predicate on worlds to every index, agree at every index
$n < d$, then for every world $w$, $\varphi$ is satisfied at $w$ in $M$ under $\mathit{env}$ if
and only if it is satisfied at $w$ in $M$ under $\mathit{env}'$.

In particular, satisfaction of a closed formula is independent of the environment.

## Sources

- D. Kozen, *Results on the propositional μ-calculus*, Theoretical Computer Science 27 (1983), 333-354.

articles.title: Size of a μ-calculus formula
articles.statement:
The size $|\varphi|$ of a μ-calculus formula $\varphi$ is
the number of nodes of its syntax tree: an atom, a negated atom, a variable, $\bot$ and $\top$
have size $1$; $|\varphi \wedge \psi| = |\varphi \vee \psi| = |\varphi| + |\psi| + 1$; and
$|\Box\varphi| = |\Diamond\varphi| = |\mu\varphi| = |\nu\varphi| = |\varphi| + 1$.

articles.title: Winning strategies stay winning along consistent moves
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Kripke model,
$\mathit{env}$ an environment and $\sigma$ a Verifier strategy for the model-checking game on
$M$. If $\sigma$ wins from a position $p$ in $\mathit{env}$, and $q$ is a position reachable from
$p$ by one move that is the position chosen by $\sigma$ at $p$ whenever Verifier owns $p$, then
$\sigma$ also wins from $q$ in $\mathit{env}$.

articles.title: Winning strategy from a position
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Kripke model, $\mathit{env}$ an environment
assigning a predicate on worlds to every index, $\sigma$ a Verifier strategy for the
model-checking game on $M$ and $p$ a game position. A play is consistent with $\sigma$ when each
step is a move and, at every Verifier-owned position, goes to the position chosen by $\sigma$.
The strategy $\sigma$ wins from $p$ in $\mathit{env}$ when every finite play from $p$ consistent
with $\sigma$ whose last position has no moves ends in a position that is a terminal win for
Verifier in $\mathit{env}$, and every infinite play from $p$ consistent with $\sigma$ satisfies
the parity condition.

articles.title: Verifier strategy
articles.statement:
A Verifier strategy for the model-checking game on a Kripke model $M$
is a map $\sigma$ from game positions to game positions such that, at every Verifier-owned
position $p$ from which some move exists, there is a move from $p$ to $\sigma(p)$.

The move-respecting condition is what makes Verifier's winning meaningful: without it, a
strategy could "win" by choosing a non-move at a Verifier position, leaving no
legal play at all.

articles.title: Winner at a terminal position
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Kripke model and $\mathit{env}$ an environment
assigning a predicate on worlds to every index. At a game position $(\varphi, w, st)$, where $st$
is the stack of enclosing fixpoint binders and $|st|$ its length, Verifier wins exactly when
$\varphi$ is an atom $a$ true at $w$, a negated atom $\neg a$ with $a$ false at $w$, $\top$, a
box $\Box\psi$, or a variable with de Bruijn index $n \ge |st|$ such that
$\mathit{env}(n - |st|)$ holds at $w$. At every other position (a variable with index
$n < |st|$, $\bot$, a diamond, a conjunction, a disjunction or a fixpoint) Refuter wins.

The condition is consulted only at positions with no moves: a box with no successors leaves
Refuter stuck and a diamond with no successors leaves Verifier stuck, while a bound variable,
a conjunction, a disjunction and a fixpoint always have a move. The environment index is
shifted by $|st|$ because each binder on the stack shifts de Bruijn indices by one.

## Sources

- C. Stirling, *Modal and Temporal Properties of Processes*, Springer 2001, Chapter 6.

articles.title: The fixpoint-free embedding is injective
articles.statement:
The embedding of fixpoint-free formulas into
μ-calculus formulas is injective: distinct fixpoint-free formulas have distinct images.

This is what lets the canonical fragment game recover a fragment formula from an
embedded game position.

articles.title: The partial inverse recovers fixpoint-free formulas
articles.statement:
For every fixpoint-free formula
$\varphi$, the partial inverse of the embedding of fixpoint-free formulas into μ-calculus
formulas is defined at the image of $\varphi$ under the embedding, with value $\varphi$.

articles.title: Partial inverse of the fixpoint-free embedding
articles.statement:
The partial map from μ-calculus formulas
to fixpoint-free formulas defined by recursion: an atom, a negated atom, $\bot$ and $\top$ are
sent to the same formula; a conjunction or disjunction is sent to the conjunction or
disjunction of the values at its two parts, and $\Box\psi$, $\Diamond\psi$ to the box or diamond
of the value at $\psi$, whenever those values are defined; the map is undefined at variables
and at least and greatest fixpoints, and at every formula with a part where it is undefined.

It inverts the embedding of fixpoint-free formulas into μ-calculus formulas on its image.

articles.title: The embedding inverts the partial inverse
articles.statement:
For every μ-calculus formula $\psi$ and every
fixpoint-free formula $\varphi$: if the partial inverse of the embedding of fixpoint-free
formulas into μ-calculus formulas is defined at $\psi$ with value $\varphi$, then the embedding
sends $\varphi$ to $\psi$.

articles.title: Embedding of the fixpoint-free fragment into the μ-calculus
articles.statement:
The map from fixpoint-free
formulas to μ-calculus formulas defined by recursion: atoms, negated atoms, $\bot$ and $\top$
go to the same atom, negated atom, $\bot$ and $\top$, and $\varphi \wedge \psi$,
$\varphi \vee \psi$, $\Box \varphi$ and $\Diamond \varphi$ go to the conjunction, disjunction,
box and diamond of the images of $\varphi$ and $\psi$.

articles.title: Game-vs-satisfaction, converse direction
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Kripke model, $\mathit{env}$ an
environment assigning a set of worlds to each variable index, $\varphi$ a fixpoint-free formula
and $w$ a world. If Verifier has a winning strategy, in environment $\mathit{env}$, in the
model-checking game on $M$ from the position made of the μ-calculus embedding of $\varphi$, the
world $w$ and the empty binder stack, then $w$ lies in the backward-induction winning region of
$\varphi$.

## Sources

- C. Stirling, *Modal and Temporal Properties of Processes*, Springer 2001, Chapter 6.

articles.title: Verifier has a winning strategy
articles.statement:
For a Kripke model $M$, an environment $\mathit{env}$
and a game position $p$, Verifier wins from $p$ when some Verifier strategy $\sigma$ in the
model-checking game on $M$ wins from $p$ in environment $\mathit{env}$: every complete finite
$\sigma$-consistent play from $p$ ends at a terminal winning position, and every infinite
$\sigma$-consistent play from $p$ satisfies the parity condition.

articles.title: The absorbing win state
articles.statement:
In the totalized fragment game on a Kripke model $M$ with
environment $\mathit{env}$, every move from the absorbing Verifier-wins state $\mathrm{win}$
leads back to it: if $\mathrm{win}$ moves to $v$, then $v = \mathrm{win}$.

articles.title: Backward-induction winning equals satisfaction on the fixpoint-free fragment
articles.statement:
For every
Kripke model $M$, environment $\mathit{env}$, fixpoint-free formula $\varphi$ and world $w$, $w$
lies in the backward-induction winning region of $\varphi$ if and only if $w$ satisfies the
μ-calculus embedding of $\varphi$ in $M$ under $\mathit{env}$.

## Sources

- C. Stirling, *Modal and Temporal Properties of Processes*, Springer 2001, Chapter 6.

articles.title: Backward-induction winning equals game winning on the fixpoint-free fragment
articles.statement:
For every
Kripke model $M$, environment $\mathit{env}$, fixpoint-free formula $\varphi$ and world $w$, $w$
lies in the backward-induction winning region of $\varphi$ if and only if Verifier has a winning
strategy, in environment $\mathit{env}$, in the model-checking game on $M$ from the position made
of the μ-calculus embedding of $\varphi$, the world $w$ and the empty binder stack.

## Sources

- C. Stirling, *Modal and Temporal Properties of Processes*, Springer 2001, Chapter 6.

articles.title: Game-vs-satisfaction, strategy direction
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Kripke model, $\mathit{env}$ an
environment assigning a set of worlds to each variable index, $\varphi$ a fixpoint-free formula
and $w$ a world in the backward-induction winning region of $\varphi$. Then Verifier has a
winning strategy, in environment $\mathit{env}$, in the model-checking game on $M$ from the
position made of the μ-calculus embedding of $\varphi$, the world $w$ and the empty binder stack.

## Sources

- C. Stirling, *Modal and Temporal Properties of Processes*, Springer 2001, Chapter 6.

articles.title: The Wins-guided move at a diamond
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Kripke model, $\varphi$ a fixpoint-free
formula and $w$ a world in the backward-induction winning region of $\Diamond \varphi$. Then
there is a successor $v$ of $w$ in $M$ lying in the backward-induction winning region of
$\varphi$ such that the Wins-guided move at the position made of the embedding of
$\Diamond \varphi$, the world $w$ and the empty binder stack is the position made of the
embedding of $\varphi$, the world $v$ and the empty stack.

articles.title: The Wins-guided move is legal
articles.statement:
For a Kripke model $M$ and a game position $p$ owned by
Verifier from which some move exists, the Wins-guided move at $p$ is a legal move of the
model-checking game on $M$ from $p$.

articles.title: The Wins-guided move at a disjunction
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Kripke model, $\varphi_1$ and
$\varphi_2$ fixpoint-free formulas and $w$ a world in the backward-induction winning region of
$\varphi_1 \vee \varphi_2$. Then for some $i \in \{1, 2\}$, $w$ lies in the backward-induction
winning region of $\varphi_i$ and the Wins-guided move at the position made of the embedding of
$\varphi_1 \vee \varphi_2$, the world $w$ and the empty binder stack is the position made of the
embedding of $\varphi_i$, the world $w$ and the empty stack.

articles.title: Wins-guided move
articles.statement:
